plain: Anthropic's 2025 chatbot family — pushed AI coding further and added the ability to handle long multi-step tasks on its own.

snappy: Anthropic's CLI-based coding agent — runs in the terminal, can read, write, and execute code in your repo.
detail: Released early 2025 as Anthropic's flagship agentic developer tool. Combines Claude's reasoning with file-system, shell, and Git access. Designed for terminal-native developers; competes with Cursor and GitHub Copilot Agent in different surface formats.
plain: Anthropic's coding helper that lives in your terminal and can read, write, and run code in your project for you.

snappy: Model that links images and text in a shared space — lets you search images by description, or steer image generators with words.
detail: OpenAI's 2021 CLIP trained a vision network and a text network side-by-side on 400 million image-caption pairs, with a loss that pulls matching pairs together and pushes mismatched pairs apart. The resulting shared space enables zero-shot image classification, text-based search, and prompt conditioning for image generators (Stable Diffusion uses CLIP for the text input).
plain: A model that learns to match pictures with their captions, so you can search images by typing a description.

snappy: AI systems whose weights and internal details are kept proprietary — accessed only through APIs or product surfaces.
detail: Frontier labs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, xAI) keep their flagship models closed. Arguments for: prevents misuse, protects investment, allows control over safety. Arguments against: concentrates power, limits independent scrutiny, prevents independent research. Most frontier capability today is closed; most volume of model deployment is increasingly open.
plain: AI whose inner workings are kept secret by the company — you can only use it through their app or website, never download it.

snappy: Renting compute, storage, and software over the internet instead of running it on hardware you own.
detail: The umbrella for AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Oracle, and the smaller specialists. Modern AI runs almost entirely on cloud infrastructure — training a frontier model requires thousands of GPUs running for months, impractical to buy outright. The market divides into hyperscalers (AWS/Azure/GCP/OCI), neoclouds (CoreWeave, Crusoe, Lambda Labs), and on-prem alternatives. Pay-by-the-hour pricing made the current AI boom economically possible.
plain: Renting computers, storage, and software over the internet rather than buying and running your own.

snappy: Fraction of a compute cluster's capacity that's actually being used productively.
detail: Hyperscalers obsess over utilization because idle GPUs are wasted capex. Modern AI clusters target 90%+ utilization. Achieved through workload mixing (training during idle hours, inference during peaks), job preemption, and tight scheduling. Major improvement metric for cloud-AI ROI calculations.
plain: How much of a giant computer farm is actually doing useful work at any moment — operators chase numbers above 90%.

snappy: Standard transistor technology for nearly all modern logic chips since the 1980s.
detail: Combines n-type and p-type transistors so that only one is conducting at a time, keeping idle power low. CMOS is what made battery-powered computing practical. Every modern CPU, GPU, and AI accelerator is built from billions of CMOS transistors.
plain: The standard recipe for making transistors used in nearly every computer chip since the 1980s — sips power when idle.

snappy: Industrial robot designed to work safely alongside humans — softer mechanisms, built-in force sensing.
detail: Pre-dates the AI-robotics wave. Universal Robots, FANUC, KUKA, ABB sell cobots for assembly, packaging, and light manufacturing. Distinguished from traditional industrial robots (faster, stronger, must be caged off) by their human-safe design. Often paired with AI-based vision and manipulation models in modern deployments.
plain: A factory robot built to work safely beside people — softer parts and sensors so it stops if it bumps into you.

snappy: Object-detection dataset — bounding boxes and segmentation masks on 330,000 everyday images.
detail: Released by Microsoft Research in 2014. The standard benchmark for object detection, instance segmentation, and image captioning for a decade. Still cited in modern vision-model evaluations alongside newer benchmarks.
plain: A free collection of 330,000 everyday photos with labels drawn around the objects — used to train and test image-recognition systems.

snappy: Tool that lets an LLM execute Python (or other code) in a sandbox to compute things, plot graphs, manipulate files.
detail: OpenAI introduced Code Interpreter (now "Advanced Data Analysis") in 2023. Claude, Gemini, and most agent frameworks now offer code execution as a standard tool. Useful for arithmetic the model would otherwise get wrong, data analysis, plotting, and running quick experiments inside the chat.
plain: A tool that lets a chatbot actually run Python code in a sandbox so it can do real math, draw graphs, or process files.

snappy: Metal plate with internal coolant channels, mounted directly on top of a chip to remove heat.
detail: Modern AI accelerators dissipate 700-1,500W per chip — too much for air cooling. Cold plates with liquid running through them are mounted directly on GPUs, CPUs, HBM stacks, and (in some designs) NVSwitches. Cold-plate quality and mounting precision affect performance: poor contact can cost a percent or two of throughput.
plain: A metal block with water running through it, pressed onto a hot chip to carry the heat away.

snappy: Renting space, power, and cooling in a third-party data center to host your own servers.
detail: AI labs that own their hardware but don't want to build buildings rent colo space from operators like Equinix, Digital Realty, CoreSite. Hybrid arrangements (some self-hosted in colo, some rented from clouds) are common. The colo industry is reshaping itself for AI: higher densities, more liquid cooling, more grid integration.
plain: Renting space inside someone else's data centre to plug in your own servers, instead of building your own building.

snappy: Public web-scrape archive — the foundation of most modern LLM training data.
detail: Non-profit organisation that has been crawling the web monthly since 2007. Each crawl is hundreds of terabytes. Almost every major LLM (GPT, Llama, Claude, Mistral) was trained on cleaned subsets of Common Crawl. Many downstream datasets (C4, RefinedWeb, FineWeb) are filtered versions of Common Crawl.
plain: A free archive of the web that's been gathered every month since 2007 — almost every big chatbot was trained on a cleaned-up slice of it.

snappy: Raw computational power — the cycles, FLOPs, and GPU-hours that AI models consume during training and inference.
detail: The single most important variable in modern AI. Measured in FLOPs (floating-point operations) for training, FLOPS/second for inference. Frontier training runs now consume 10^25 FLOPs — equivalent to running every desktop CPU on Earth for years. Compute scaling has driven every major capability leap since 2018. Access to compute (via hyperscalers, neoclouds, or owned clusters) is now a primary moat in the AI industry; export controls, GPU shortages, and gigawatt-scale data centres are downstream consequences.
plain: Raw computing power — the number-crunching that AI uses up while training and answering questions.

snappy: Process — formal or informal — by which a lab's compute budget is divided among teams, projects, and experiments.
detail: Major operational question for any AI lab. Frontier labs report compute allocation as one of the most consequential management decisions: who gets to train, with how many GPUs, for how long. Often handled via internal bidding, dedicated allocation councils, or top-down strategy decisions.
plain: How an AI lab decides which teams get how much of the precious computing power, and for how long.

snappy: Many connected servers working as a single logical computer — the basic unit of AI training infrastructure.
detail: A modern AI training cluster might have hundreds to tens of thousands of GPUs spread across many servers, all connected by high-bandwidth networking. The cluster runs distributed training jobs that coordinate across all nodes. Building and operating clusters at scale is a major engineering challenge — hardware failures are constant, jobs need to checkpoint and recover.
plain: A roomful of servers wired together so they act like one giant computer — the workhorse of AI training.

snappy: Policy approach: regulate AI by regulating access to large amounts of training compute.
detail: Argument: compute is concentrated, hard to hide, and roughly correlates with capability — so it's a leverage point. The US October 2023 executive order's reporting requirements above 10²⁶ FLOPs (and the EU AI Act's 10²⁵ threshold) put compute at the centre of frontier-AI governance. Critics worry the threshold is arbitrary and that algorithmic improvements will route around it.
plain: Regulating AI by limiting who's allowed to use very large amounts of computing power — since big computers are hard to hide.

snappy: A workload limited by the speed of math operations, not memory access.
detail: Large-batch training is often compute-bound: GPUs can keep their math units fed because they reuse weights across many examples. Most LLM inference is the opposite — memory-bound, because each new token requires reading the whole model. Knowing which regime you're in determines which optimisations help (more compute? more bandwidth? better caching?).
plain: A job whose speed is limited by how fast the chip can do math, not by how fast it can fetch data from memory.

snappy: The sweet spot in the trade-off between model size and training-token count for a fixed compute budget.
detail: Chinchilla suggested roughly 20 tokens per parameter is compute-optimal — i.e., for a 7B model, train on ~140B tokens. Later work (Llama 3, several papers) revised the figure upward to 50-100+ tokens/param when inference cost matters: it's worth over-training a model so you don't have to serve a huge one. Modern frontier models are heavily over-trained relative to Chinchilla.
plain: The best balance between making a model bigger and feeding it more training text, for a fixed budget of computing power.

snappy: Tool that gives an agent control of a virtual computer — moving the mouse, typing, clicking, reading the screen.
detail: Anthropic released Computer Use as an API feature in late 2024; OpenAI followed with Operator. The model receives screenshots, decides on actions, and the system executes them. Early but transformative: lets agents drive software designed for humans, no API required. Slow and error-prone today; rapidly improving.
plain: Giving an AI control of a virtual computer — letting it move the mouse, click buttons, and type, just like a person would.

snappy: The branch of AI that processes images and video — recognition, detection, segmentation, generation, and understanding of visual content.
detail: Dominated by convolutional neural networks from 2012 (AlexNet on ImageNet) through the late 2010s, then by Vision Transformers and multimodal models from ~2020 onward. Applications span face recognition, self-driving cars, medical imaging, content moderation, and generative tasks (Stable Diffusion, Sora). Often combined with NLP into vision-language models (VLMs) like CLIP, GPT-4o, and Claude that can reason about both modalities.
plain: The branch of AI that handles pictures and video — recognising faces, spotting objects, or making new images.

snappy: Table showing prediction outcomes — true positives, false positives, true negatives, false negatives.
detail: Foundational diagnostic for classification problems. Used to derive most other classification metrics (accuracy, precision, recall, F1). Heat-map visualisations are standard in ML reports. Helps identify which classes a model confuses with which others.
plain: A small grid that shows where a model got things right and wrong — handy for spotting which categories it mixes up.

snappy: Anthropic's approach to alignment — the model is shown a written list of principles and trained to critique itself against them.
detail: Instead of asking humans to rate every response, the model is given a "constitution" — a list of principles like "be helpful", "don't help with harm", "avoid stereotypes". The model generates a response, then critiques and rewrites it against those principles. Used to train Claude. The aim is to make alignment more transparent (the principles are written down) and scalable (humans don't need to rate every output).
plain: Anthropic's training method where the model is given a written list of rules and taught to check its own answers against them.

snappy: Forcing model output to match a specific format — grammar, JSON schema, regex, or finite-state machine.
detail: Implemented at the sampling step: at each token, only allow choices consistent with the grammar. Used heavily for structured output, code generation in specific languages, and any place downstream code needs reliably-formatted text. Outlines, Guidance, and Microsoft's TypeChat are common open-source implementations.
plain: Forcing a model's output to follow a specific shape — like always producing valid JSON — by blocking any tokens that would break the format.

snappy: Lightweight virtualization — packages an app with all its dependencies into an isolated, portable unit.
detail: Docker popularised the format. Modern AI services run as containers because they bring a fixed environment (CUDA version, framework version, Python version) to whatever host machine they land on. Kubernetes orchestrates containers; CRI-O and containerd are common container runtimes underneath.
plain: A neat package of an app with everything it needs to run, so it behaves the same wherever you drop it.

snappy: The maximum amount of text a model can hold in mind at once, measured in tokens.
detail: Bounded by attention's quadratic memory cost. Early GPT models had 2,000–4,000-token windows; GPT-4 expanded to 128,000; Claude 3.5 to 200,000; Gemini 1.5 to 1 million-plus. Longer windows let you stuff more context (whole books, long codebases) but inference cost rises with window length, and models often struggle to use very long contexts evenly — the "lost in the middle" effect.
plain: How much text a model can keep in mind at once, measured in tokens — anything beyond it gets forgotten.

snappy: Training an already-trained model on new data — extending its knowledge, language coverage, or skills.
detail: Used to update a base model with newer web data, add a new language, or extend domain coverage. Risks catastrophic forgetting of original capabilities; mitigated by mixing in some original training data. Practical importance: full retraining of frontier models is prohibitive, so labs continually post-train instead.
plain: Taking an already-trained model and teaching it new things — like fresher news or a new language — without starting over.

snappy: Inference scheduling where finished requests are replaced mid-batch — keeps the GPU full when requests have different lengths.
detail: Standard batching waits for the longest request in a batch to finish before starting new ones, wasting compute. Continuous batching adds new prompts to the batch as soon as slots open, dramatically improving throughput for chat-like workloads with varying response lengths. The headline innovation behind vLLM and now standard across inference engines.
plain: A scheduling trick where finished requests are swapped out mid-stream so the GPU never sits idle waiting for the slowest one.

snappy: Self-supervised technique — train an embedding model by pulling matching pairs (image, caption) together and pushing non-matching pairs apart.
detail: Powers CLIP (image-text), SimCLR (image-image), SimCSE (sentence-sentence), and many other foundation models. The InfoNCE loss is the standard objective. Effective at producing semantically meaningful embeddings that work well in downstream tasks.
plain: Training a model by showing it matching pairs and mismatched pairs, and teaching it to pull matches close and shove mismatches apart.

snappy: Add-on to diffusion image generators that lets you condition output on a pose, depth map, edge map, or other structure.
detail: Released 2023. Lets you generate an image of a specific subject in a specific pose by giving the model a stick-figure or depth map alongside the prompt. Open-source. Hugely popular in the Stable Diffusion community because it gave creators much finer control over generation than text alone.
plain: An add-on for image generators that lets you control the pose or shape of what's drawn, not just describe it in words.

snappy: Whether the loss surface has a single global minimum (convex) or many local minima and saddle points (non-convex).
detail: Linear and logistic regression have convex losses — gradient descent finds the global optimum. Deep neural networks are wildly non-convex. Empirically, this matters less than classical theory predicted: deep networks find good (often near-global) solutions by gradient descent, despite the loss landscape being complicated.
plain: Whether a model's error landscape has one clear lowest point (convex) or lots of dips and bumps that can trap the search (non-convex).

snappy: Type of network built for images — it slides small pattern detectors across the input to pick up local features.
detail: CNNs dominated computer vision from AlexNet (2012) through the late 2010s — face recognition, object detection, image classification. They're naturally suited to images because the same small filter can find an edge or a texture anywhere in the picture. Vision Transformers have since matched or beaten them on most benchmarks, but CNNs are still the default for vision on phones and small chips.
plain: A type of neural network for images — it slides small pattern detectors across the picture to find edges, textures, and shapes.

snappy: Heat exchanger that interfaces between the facility's chilled water and the cold plates inside servers.
detail: Each rack typically has its own CDU. The facility water loop runs at moderate temperatures; the chip-loop is isolated and runs cooler and cleaner. CDU capacity scales with rack power density — modern AI racks need CDUs sized for 100+ kW of heat removal.
plain: A heat exchanger that sits inside a server rack and shuttles heat from the chips out to the building's chilled water.

snappy: Generic term for an AI assistant that works alongside you, suggesting completions or actions.
detail: Branded by GitHub Copilot (2021), the first widely-used AI coding assistant powered by OpenAI Codex. Microsoft adopted the term across products: M365 Copilot, Windows Copilot, GitHub Copilot Agent. Now used loosely for any chat-based AI workflow assistant.
plain: A generic name for an AI helper that sits beside you while you work and suggests what to do next.

snappy: GPU-specialised cloud — rents H100s and B200s to AI labs and enterprises that the hyperscalers can't serve fast enough.
detail: Started as a crypto miner, pivoted to AI in 2022. Now public (IPO 2024). Built around aggressive GPU acquisition and a software stack focused on AI workloads. Major customers include Microsoft (offloading some OpenAI training), and many AI startups that need NVIDIA capacity now rather than waiting in a hyperscaler queue.
plain: A cloud company specialising in renting out top-end NVIDIA GPUs to AI labs that can't get them anywhere else fast enough.

snappy: NVIDIA's platform for training physical-AI foundation models — provides simulation, data, and pretrained world models.
detail: Announced January 2025. Includes pretrained world-models (predicts how scenes evolve given actions), simulation tooling, and data pipelines tuned for robotics. Positioning: the equivalent of CUDA + PyTorch but for physical AI. Used by Figure, 1X, Agility, and many other robotics developers.
plain: NVIDIA's toolkit for training AIs that understand the physical world — aimed at robot makers.
TSMC's way of putting laser-based optical communication chips right next to compute chips in the same package.
snappy: TSMC's silicon-photonics integration platform — co-packaging optical I/O alongside compute chips in advanced packages.
detail: It brings optical engines into the CoWoS-style package, reducing electrical-to-optical conversion loss versus pluggable optics. TSMC announced CoUPe progress at OCP and other forums in 2025-26 alongside customer-specific projects. Expected to enable next-generation AI rack-scale designs where bandwidth between compute and switch fabric exceeds copper's reach. Adjacent to but separate from Co-Packaged Optics solutions from Broadcom and others.

snappy: TSMC's flagship advanced packaging — places multiple dies (compute, memory) onto a silicon interposer.
detail: Used in NVIDIA H100, H200, B200, AMD MI300/350, Google TPU v4/v5/Trillium, and most other high-end AI accelerators. The HBM memory stacks sit right next to the compute die on the interposer, enabling huge bandwidth. CoWoS capacity is TSMC-limited and remains the binding constraint on frontier-AI chip supply.
plain: TSMC's advanced way of packaging a chip — stacking the compute and memory chips side by side on one slab for huge speed.
The single number — how many CoWoS-packaged chips TSMC can build per month — that determines how many AI accelerators the world can have.
snappy: TSMC's monthly wafer-equivalent throughput for CoWoS packaging — the binding constraint on AI accelerator supply through 2026.
detail: TSMC's CoWoS lines run from a few thousand wafer-equivalents per month in 2022 to a 2026 target around 75,000 and 2027 plans above 130,000. NVIDIA and AMD compete for allocation; smaller customers wait months. The capacity number drives quarterly AI hardware availability and is the most cited supply metric in industry analyst coverage. Building it requires new TSMC buildings plus equipment from a thin supplier base.

plain: A newer way of building giant chip packages bigger than a single piece of silicon could ever be.
snappy: Larger CoWoS variant using local silicon bridges instead of a single full-size interposer — enabling packages bigger than a reticle.
detail: It removes the single-die size limit of CoWoS-S by stitching small silicon bridges (LSI) into an organic substrate. NVIDIA's Blackwell B200 was the first volume product on CoWoS-L, integrating two reticle-sized GPU dies plus eight HBM3e stacks. Rubin and Rubin Ultra extend the technique further. The trade-off is more complex assembly versus more die area per package.

plain: A cheaper version of CoWoS that uses simpler organic materials instead of a costly silicon base, traded against less performance.
snappy: Cost-reduced CoWoS variant that replaces the silicon interposer with an organic redistribution film (RDL).
detail: Organic redistribution structures are cheaper and easier to manufacture than silicon interposers but carry less bandwidth and fewer connections. CoWoS-R targets mid-tier AI accelerators and high-end CPUs where the full CoWoS-S bandwidth is not needed but cost matters. AMD has used variants of this approach for several MI- and Instinct-line products. Helps TSMC stretch packaging capacity across more price points.

plain: The most common technique for connecting AI compute chips and high-speed memory together on a shared silicon base.
snappy: Original TSMC CoWoS variant using a silicon interposer to wire compute dies and HBM stacks together at very high bandwidth.
detail: CoWoS-S has carried every major AI accelerator from V100 onward — H100, MI300X, GH200 all use it. The silicon interposer is itself a chip-sized piece of silicon with fine-pitch wiring. Capacity at TSMC is the binding constraint on AI hardware supply through 2026, with TSMC investing aggressively to expand it. CoWoS-L is the larger-than-reticle variant; CoWoS-R is the cost-down RDL variant.

snappy: The general-purpose processor at the heart of every computer — good at everything, great at nothing in particular.
detail: CPUs run the operating system, schedule tasks, and handle the kinds of branchy logic GPUs are bad at. Modern server CPUs (Intel Xeon, AMD EPYC, AWS Graviton) have 32-128 cores. AI workloads mostly run on GPUs but the CPU still hosts the show: loading data, coordinating between accelerators, running pre/post-processing. Inference of small models can run perfectly well on CPU.
plain: The general-purpose processor at the heart of every computer — decent at everything, not specialised for any one thing.

snappy: Attention pattern that mixes information from two different sequences — encoder output and decoder hidden state, image patches and text tokens.
detail: How conditioning works in many architectures: the encoder produces a representation, the decoder cross-attends to it while generating. Used in encoder-decoder Transformers (T5), image generators (Stable Diffusion cross-attends to text), and any multimodal system that fuses inputs.
plain: A way for one part of a model to peek at and mix in information from a different stream — like text guiding image generation.

snappy: Loss function used in classification and language modelling — penalises probability mass placed on the wrong answer.
detail: If the right answer has probability p under the model, cross-entropy loss is -log(p). The lower the probability the model assigned to the correct token, the larger the loss. Equivalent to maximising the log-likelihood of the training data. Standard objective for next-token prediction during pretraining.
plain: The standard scoring rule that punishes a model harder the lower the probability it gave to the right answer.

snappy: Technique for measuring model performance — split data into K folds and train K models, each leaving one fold out for testing.
detail: Gives a more reliable performance estimate than a single train/test split, at K× the compute cost. Standard for hyperparameter tuning and model selection on small-to-medium datasets. Less common in frontier deep learning because training runs are too expensive to repeat.
plain: Splitting your data into chunks, training on most of them, testing on the leftover one, and repeating — gives a fairer score than a single test.

snappy: AI infrastructure company building data centers next to stranded energy sources (oil flares, renewables).
detail: Originally built modular data centres at oil-and-gas sites to use flare gas that would otherwise burn off. Now pivoting to large-scale AI infrastructure with sites in Iceland, Texas, and elsewhere. Partner on the Stargate project. The thesis: cheap power is the binding constraint on AI infrastructure, and Crusoe finds it where others don't look.
plain: An infrastructure company that builds data centres next to leftover energy — flared gas or remote renewables — to get cheap power.

snappy: NVIDIA's programming model and software stack for running general-purpose code on GPUs — the moat.
detail: Released in 2007. CUDA lets you write code that runs on the thousands of cores inside an NVIDIA GPU. Every major AI framework (PyTorch, TensorFlow, JAX) sits on top of CUDA. The ecosystem of CUDA libraries, kernels, and developer tools is NVIDIA's single biggest competitive advantage — competitors (AMD ROCm, Apple MLX, Intel oneAPI) keep trying to catch up.
plain: NVIDIA's software toolkit that lets developers run code on GPUs — the thing rivals have spent two decades trying to copy.

snappy: The general-purpose compute units in NVIDIA GPUs — handle everything that isn't a tensor-core matrix multiply.
detail: Each modern NVIDIA GPU has thousands of CUDA cores running in parallel (an H100 has over 16,000). They run regular floating-point arithmetic and are what gets used for the parts of a workload that aren't matrix multiplies — activations, normalisations, indexing, custom kernels. Tensor cores do the heavy lifting; CUDA cores do everything else.
plain: The general-purpose calculator inside an NVIDIA GPU — handles all the regular math that isn't a giant matrix multiplication.

snappy: NVIDIA's optimised primitives for the operations that show up in every neural network.
detail: Sits below frameworks like PyTorch. Provides hand-tuned implementations of convolution, attention, matrix multiplication, normalisation, and activation functions, each squeezed for maximum throughput on whichever NVIDIA GPU you happen to have. Major contributor to why a PyTorch model runs faster on NVIDIA than on competing hardware with software-equivalent stacks.
plain: NVIDIA's library of hand-tuned shortcuts for the common operations every neural network uses — squeezes maximum speed out of the hardware.

snappy: Training strategy — present the model with easier examples first, then progressively harder ones.
detail: Inspired by how humans learn. In LLM training, this might mean training on cleaner web text first, then noisier crawls; or simple math problems before competition-grade ones. Effective when used carefully; tricky to get the difficulty ordering right. Reasoning-model training uses curriculum approaches over chains of thought.
plain: Training a model by giving it easy examples first and harder ones later — much like how people learn.

snappy: AI-first code editor — fork of VS Code with deep integration of large language models.
detail: Built by Anysphere, founded 2022. Made Claude and GPT integrations central to the coding workflow: tab-complete, chat with codebase, agentic refactors. Reached major adoption in 2024-2025 as one of the standout AI productivity tools. Often used with Claude as the underlying model.
plain: A code editor built around AI — a souped-up version of VS Code where the chatbot is woven into how you write code.
An HBM stack where the bottom control chip is custom-designed for one specific buyer like NVIDIA or AMD, instead of being off-the-shelf.
snappy: An HBM4-era trend where the base die under an HBM stack is built to the buyer's specification on a foundry logic process.
detail: Whereas standard HBM is a commodity, a custom HBM base die can integrate buyer-specific controller logic, error-correction tuning, or test hooks. NVIDIA and AMD are both reportedly designing custom base dies for HBM4 variants of Rubin and MI400. Restructures HBM economics: the DRAM stack remains a memory-maker product but the base die is co-designed with the accelerator vendor and built at TSMC.

snappy: Newer interconnect standard built on PCIe — adds cache-coherent memory sharing between CPUs and accelerators.
detail: CXL 2.0 and 3.0 enable memory pooling: one server can share its memory with another over CXL, or attach external memory modules that look like RAM to the CPU. AMD, Intel, NVIDIA, Microsoft, and Google all back the standard. Slower deployment than originally hoped but expected to reshape data-centre memory architectures in the late 2020s.
plain: A newer plumbing standard that lets a computer's main chip and its accelerators share the same pool of memory.
A way of adding extra memory to a server through a flexible cable-like connection, instead of plugging it directly into the motherboard.
snappy: Memory expansion or pooling that connects to a CPU over the CXL interface instead of a DDR channel — adds capacity at the cost of latency.
detail: CXL.mem lets servers attach DRAM via PCIe-class lanes rather than direct DDR sockets. Useful for memory-tier expansion (cheap, lots of it) and for pooling memory across many servers in a rack. Microsoft and Meta have both published deployment results. Higher latency than direct DDR limits its use for hot inference paths; cold KV-cache and large embedding tables are the natural fits.

snappy: OpenAI's text-to-image model family — released January 2021 (DALL-E 1), then DALL-E 2 (2022), DALL-E 3 (2023).
detail: Pioneered the modern era of generative image AI. DALL-E 3 introduced in-context refinement via ChatGPT and significant quality improvement. Eventually subsumed into GPT-4o's native image generation (March 2025) which produces images directly from the chat model rather than calling a separate image model.
plain: OpenAI's family of image-making models — type a description, get a picture back.

snappy: Producing more training data by transforming existing examples — rotating images, paraphrasing text, adding noise.
detail: Standard practice in image classification (random crops, flips, colour jitter, RandAugment), speech (noise, time-stretching), and text (synonym replacement, back-translation). Improves model robustness and effective training-set size. Modern foundation models rely on heavy augmentation in pretraining.
plain: Squeezing more training examples out of what you have by tweaking copies — flipping photos, rephrasing sentences, adding noise.

snappy: A building purpose-built for housing servers, storage, and networking equipment at scale.
detail: Modern AI training data centers are enormous: tens or hundreds of megawatts of power, thousands of GPUs, kilometres of fibre. The biggest single-site builds (xAI's Memphis facility, Microsoft/OpenAI's Stargate, Meta's Mesa) approach 1 GW. Site selection driven by cheap electricity, cooling water, and fast fibre access — Texas, Iowa, Northern Virginia, and the Nordics are AI hotspots.
plain: A purpose-built warehouse packed with servers, storage, and networking gear that runs the internet's heavy lifting.

snappy: Process of selecting which content from a raw web scrape is worth training on.
detail: Modern frontier pretraining is shaped more by data filtering decisions than by architecture. Common filters: language identification, quality scoring (perplexity, classifier-based), deduplication, toxic-content removal, personal-data scrubbing, copyright stripping. Each lab's filtering recipe is treated as a trade secret.
plain: Sifting through a giant pile of scraped web pages and keeping only the bits worth learning from.

snappy: Legal agreements covering the use of copyrighted content in AI training data.
detail: OpenAI's deals with the AP, FT, News Corp, Vox Media; Google's deal with Reddit; Anthropic and others have similar deals. Lawsuits from the New York Times, music labels, and others continue. The 2023-2025 era is establishing whether training on copyrighted content is fair use, and at what licensing cost it can or must be acquired.
plain: Legal deals that grant permission to use copyrighted books, articles, or images as training material.

snappy: Each GPU holds a full copy of the model and works on a different slice of the batch — the simplest parallel setup.
detail: After every step, GPUs exchange gradients so they stay synchronised. Easy to implement and scales linearly up to maybe 100 GPUs. Beyond that, the communication overhead and memory cost of replicating the model become prohibitive — bigger models switch to tensor/pipeline parallelism or sharded variants like FSDP.
plain: The simplest way to split training across many GPUs — give each one a full copy and a different chunk of examples.

snappy: Specifying where a user's data is physically stored — finer-grained than sovereignty.
detail: Enterprise customers often require contractual guarantees that their data stays in specific regions (e.g., "EU-only processing for GDPR compliance"). Hyperscalers offer region-locked services for this; AI labs increasingly add geographic data-handling commitments. Important compliance and procurement category.
plain: A guarantee about which country, region, or city a customer's data physically lives in.

snappy: Legal requirement that data stays within a specific country's borders.
detail: Many jurisdictions (EU under GDPR, China, Russia, India for certain data classes) require data to be stored and processed locally. Drives demand for in-country cloud regions and local AI infrastructure. Sovereign-AI initiatives (France's Mistral, UAE's G42, India's various LLM projects) are partly responses to data-sovereignty concerns.
plain: A legal rule saying certain kinds of data must stay inside a country's borders.

snappy: A collection of data used to train, evaluate, or test a model — the raw material from which AI systems learn.
detail: Quality and scale both matter. Frontier LLMs train on trillions of tokens scraped from the web (Common Crawl, FineWeb), books (Books3), code (The Stack), and curated mixtures. Computer vision models use ImageNet, COCO, LAION. Benchmark datasets (MMLU, HumanEval, GPQA) measure capability rather than provide training data. Data licensing, copyright, and contamination (test data leaking into training) are central debates.
plain: A collection of examples used to teach or test a model — the raw material it learns from.

snappy: Early actor-critic algorithm for continuous-action environments — RL for steering, throttle, joint torques.
detail: Introduced 2015. Bridged discrete-action methods (DQN) with continuous-action problems by using a deterministic policy. Brittle in practice — sensitive to hyperparameters. TD3 and SAC are improved successors that addressed DDPG's training instability.
plain: An older method for teaching agents to control things with smooth dials, like steering a car or moving a robot arm.

snappy: Hypothetical failure mode where a model pretends to be aligned during training in order to gain trust, then defects later.
detail: Closely related to scheming. Currently theoretical for production models but plausible for sufficiently capable agents. Anthropic, OpenAI, and DeepMind have all published research on detecting deceptive behaviour in current models — a precursor to ensuring it can be detected in more capable future ones.
plain: A worrying possibility: a model behaves well while being watched, then misbehaves once it thinks it can get away with it.

snappy: Classifier that asks a series of yes/no questions about features to arrive at a prediction.
detail: Intuitive, interpretable, but prone to overfitting on its own. The basic building block of more powerful ensemble methods (random forests, gradient boosting). Still used standalone when interpretability matters more than accuracy.
plain: A predictor that asks a chain of yes/no questions about your data and lands on an answer at the bottom.

snappy: The part of a model that writes its output one word at a time, each word built on what's come before.
detail: Decoders can only look backward, never forward — necessary for left-to-right generation. Today's chatbots (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama, Grok) are all decoder-only Transformers; they've absorbed the encoder's job into a single stack. This makes them simpler to train at scale and is one reason the decoder-only architecture has dominated since GPT-3.
plain: The part of a model that writes its answer one word at a time, each word building on the words before it.

snappy: The general process of turning a model's predictions into an output sequence.
detail: Covers everything from greedy decoding through beam search and various sampling strategies. The choice of decoding strategy can have a bigger effect on output quality than people realise — the same model can feel completely different with different decoding settings. Modern chat APIs expose temperature, top-p, and a few other dials.
plain: The process of turning a model's raw predictions into an actual sentence the user reads.

snappy: Removing duplicate or near-duplicate documents from a training corpus.
detail: Improves both training efficiency and final model quality. Naive duplicates (same URL, exact byte match) are easy; near-duplicates (paraphrases, copy-pasted blog posts) need fuzzy methods like MinHash. Heavy deduplication is one of the biggest separators between high-quality and low-quality LLM corpora.
plain: Stripping out duplicate or nearly-identical pages from a training pile so the model doesn't waste time re-reading the same thing.

snappy: Machine learning using neural networks with many layers — the approach behind essentially all modern AI breakthroughs.
detail: The "deep" refers to network depth (many stacked layers), which lets models learn hierarchical representations — early layers detect edges, deeper ones detect faces. Took off in 2012 when GPUs made training large networks practical (AlexNet on ImageNet). Encompasses convolutional, recurrent, and transformer architectures. Distinguishes itself from classical ML (random forests, SVMs) by learning features directly from raw data rather than relying on hand-engineered ones.
plain: The flavour of machine learning that uses many-layered neural networks — the engine behind almost every recent AI breakthrough.

snappy: Reinforcement learning that uses deep neural networks as the function approximator — the combination that powered AlphaGo, AlphaZero, and modern RLHF.
detail: Pre-2013, RL worked with hand-engineered features and small state spaces. The breakthrough came when DeepMind's DQN learned to play Atari from raw pixels (2013). Powered every major RL milestone since: AlphaGo (2016) beating Lee Sedol, AlphaZero mastering chess and shogi from self-play, AlphaStar in StarCraft II, robotic locomotion and dexterity, and the alignment phase of frontier LLMs via RLHF and DPO. The "deep" supplies pattern recognition; the "RL" supplies the learn-by-reward loop.
plain: Combining trial-and-error learning with deep neural networks — the recipe behind AlphaGo and modern chatbot fine-tuning.

snappy: AI-generated image, audio, or video that convincingly impersonates a real person.
detail: Initially face-swap videos in 2017; now any synthetic media that misrepresents real people. Used for non-consensual imagery, election misinformation, financial fraud (voice cloning), and impersonation scams. Laws criminalising specific uses (intimate-image deepfakes, election deepfakes) are proliferating in 2024-2025 across many jurisdictions.
plain: A fake image, audio clip, or video made by AI that convincingly impersonates a real person.

snappy: Chinese AI lab — released open-weight V3 and reasoning model R1 that punched well above expected weight.
detail: Founded 2023 by a Chinese hedge fund executive. Released DeepSeek-V3 (late 2024) and R1 (Jan 2025) with claims of dramatically lower training cost than US frontier models. The releases sparked debates about whether the US lead in AI compute was as durable as assumed.
plain: A Chinese AI lab that surprised the industry by releasing strong open models built much more cheaply than rivals.

snappy: Chinese open-weight reasoning model released January 2025 — first open competitor to OpenAI's o1.
detail: Demonstrated that reinforcement learning over chains of thought could produce strong reasoning in a relatively small, fully open model. Built on the DeepSeek-V3 base. The release moved markets — NVIDIA stock dropped sharply on the news as investors questioned whether frontier AI required the previously-assumed compute budgets.
plain: A Chinese open model released in January 2025 that thinks step-by-step before answering — the first real rival to OpenAI's o1.

snappy: Chinese open-weight MoE model released late 2024 — competitive with GPT-4o at a fraction of the training cost.
detail: 671B total parameters, 37B active per token. Reportedly trained for roughly $5.6M on 2,000 H800 GPUs over 2 months. Strong on reasoning, coding, and math. Sparked extensive discussion of how cheaply frontier-class models could be trained. Sister reasoning model R1 (early 2025) also generated headlines.
plain: A Chinese open model from late 2024 that matched GPT-4o quality while reportedly costing a tiny fraction to train.

snappy: Microsoft's library for training huge models on commodity clusters — home of the ZeRO optimiser.
detail: Implements ZeRO (sharded data parallelism), pipeline parallelism, mixed precision, and many other distributed training optimisations. Built on top of PyTorch. Critical infrastructure for training models in the 100B-1T parameter range without buying NVIDIA's premium DGX systems.
plain: A Microsoft toolkit that helps researchers train huge models across many GPUs without buying premium hardware.
How many tiny manufacturing flaws appear on each wafer — the smaller this number, the more chips actually work.
snappy: Defects per square centimetre of finished wafer — the underlying number that determines yield at a given chip size.
detail: Lower defect density means larger chips can be built without one fatal flaw landing on each die. TSMC famously publishes a defect-density chart for each new node as it ramps; flat or declining curves signal a healthy ramp. It is the binding constraint on big-die designs like Blackwell B200 and Rubin, where a single bad spot can ruin a 800-1500mm² die.

snappy: Earlier rule of thumb that said as transistors got smaller, they also got proportionally faster and more power-efficient.
detail: Held from the 1970s until about 2005. Then voltage stopped scaling down with size, so each shrink no longer gave the same power benefit. End of Dennard scaling is why CPU clock speeds plateaued around 4 GHz and why the industry shifted to multi-core and specialised accelerators.
plain: An old rule that said shrinking transistors also made them faster and more power-efficient — it stopped working around 2005.

snappy: Inferring 3D distance to each pixel from a single 2D image — a notoriously hard problem.
detail: Pre-deep-learning approaches barely worked. Modern depth models (DepthAnything, MiDaS, Marigold) give surprisingly good results from a single photo. Used in AR effects (portrait mode), robotics (perception without Lidar), 3D scene reconstruction, AI image editing.
plain: Guessing how far away each pixel in a single photo really is — surprisingly hard but now done well by modern models.

snappy: Autonomous coding agent from Cognition Labs — frames AI as a "software engineer" rather than an assistant.
detail: Launched March 2024 with demos of multi-hour, multi-step coding tasks. Spawned debate about how autonomous coding agents would work in practice. Pricing aimed at enterprise. The product remains active; a category of "agent SWE" startups has grown around the concept.
plain: A coding assistant from Cognition Labs marketed as an autonomous software engineer rather than a helper.

snappy: NVIDIA's pre-built AI server systems — racks of GPUs with networking and storage included.
detail: DGX H100 is a single chassis with 8 H100s connected by NVSwitch. DGX SuperPOD links many DGX nodes into a multi-thousand-GPU cluster. NVIDIA also sells DGX Cloud, which rents these systems by the hour. The DGX brand carries premium pricing but takes the integration headaches off the customer.
plain: NVIDIA's pre-assembled AI servers — racks already wired up with GPUs, networking, and storage.

snappy: An individual chip — the rectangular piece you get when a finished wafer is cut into pieces.
detail: An H100 die is about 814 mm² (huge — limited by the reticle size of the lithography equipment). A consumer mobile SoC die is around 100 mm². Larger dies cost more (fewer per wafer, lower yield) but enable bigger, more powerful chips. Advanced packaging (CoWoS, chiplets) lets multiple dies act as one.
plain: A single finished chip — the small rectangle cut from a circular silicon disc once manufacturing is done.

snappy: Generic term for the wiring between chiplets in a package — UCIe, Infinity Fabric, NVLink-C2C, BoW are specific instances.
detail: Modern chiplet designs have died-to-die bandwidth measured in TB/s. The standards body battle (UCIe vs proprietary protocols like NVLink) is one of the strategic fronts in chip-platform competition. Open standards favor a healthy ecosystem; proprietary protocols favor incumbents.
plain: The tiny wiring that links several small chips packaged together so they can act as one big chip.
A way of bonding individual chips onto a silicon base one at a time — slower but easier to control quality.
snappy: Hybrid bonding method that places known-good individual dies onto a base wafer one-by-one — slower but more flexible than wafer-to-wafer.
detail: Each die is tested and aligned individually before bonding, which lets the assembly mix die sizes and known-good-only parts. The throughput cost is higher per bond, but yield risk is lower for expensive compute dies. Used for stacking compute dies onto HBM base dies and similar mixed-size assemblies. The 'flexible' variant of hybrid bonding versus the 'high-throughput' wafer-to-wafer flavour.

snappy: Mathematical guarantee that a model's outputs don't reveal too much about any single training example.
detail: Achieved by adding calibrated noise during training. Apple uses it heavily for on-device telemetry. Important for AI training on sensitive data (medical, financial). Trade-off: stronger privacy guarantees mean worse model performance. Implemented in PyTorch via Opacus.
plain: A mathematical promise that a model's answers won't leak details about any specific person in its training data.

snappy: Generative model that learns to turn random static into a real-looking image by removing noise step by step.
detail: Training works by taking an image, adding random noise until it's pure static, and teaching the model to reverse one step of that process. At generation time, the model starts from noise and denoises iteratively to produce a fresh image. DALL-E 3, Stable Diffusion, Flux, Midjourney, and OpenAI's video model Sora all work this way. Diffusion is now spreading to audio, video, and even text.
plain: An image generator that learns to turn random visual static into a real-looking picture by cleaning it up step by step.

snappy: Architecture combining transformer backbones with diffusion training — used in modern image and video generators.
detail: Released 2022 by Berkeley/Meta. Replaces the U-Net commonly used in diffusion with a transformer. Scales better and produces higher-quality samples. Used in Sora, Stable Diffusion 3, Flux, and most modern image/video generators. Indicates the gradual convergence of vision and language architectures.
plain: An image and video generator that pairs a transformer brain with the noise-removal trick of a diffusion model.

snappy: Training a small model to mimic the outputs of a large one — cheaper to run, often surprisingly good.
detail: The large "teacher" model produces outputs (or probability distributions) on a big set of prompts. The small "student" is trained to match them. Distilled models capture most of the teacher's capabilities at a fraction of the cost. GPT-4o mini, Claude Haiku, and Gemini Flash are all distilled from larger siblings. Phi-3 is a notable open-source example.
plain: Training a small, cheap model to copy the answers of a big, expensive one — you keep most of the smarts at much lower cost.

snappy: When the data a model sees in deployment differs from the data it was trained on — a major source of failures.
detail: An AI trained on photos from sunny California will struggle in snowy Sweden. An LLM trained on web text through 2024 will be confused by 2026 events. Distribution shift is the deep reason model performance often degrades after deployment. Distinct from but related to dataset bias.
plain: When the world a model sees in real use looks different from the world it was trained on — a common cause of failures.

snappy: Tesla's custom AI training accelerator, built specifically for self-driving and humanoid-robot training.
detail: Each Dojo "D1" chip is custom silicon manufactured by TSMC. Cabinets combine many of them into "tiles" and then full systems. Tesla deploys Dojo as part of its training infrastructure for FSD and Optimus alongside large NVIDIA H100/B200 clusters. Existence and roadmap occasionally clouded by mixed signals from Tesla leadership.
plain: Tesla's custom-built training computer, designed specifically to teach its self-driving cars and humanoid robots.

snappy: Allen Institute for AI's open 3-trillion-token dataset — released with full documentation and OLMo models.
detail: Released 2024. Sourced from Common Crawl, Reddit, books, code, scientific papers. Hallmark: extreme transparency — every filtering decision documented, full reproducibility commitment. Backbone of OLMo (Open Language Model) project. Demonstrates the case for fully-open, auditable training data.
plain: The Allen Institute's huge, fully-documented training dataset, released alongside its open OLMo models.

snappy: Implanting specific atoms (boron, phosphorus, arsenic) into silicon to change its electrical properties.
detail: Pure silicon doesn't conduct well. Doping converts regions into n-type (extra electrons) or p-type (electron holes), creating the contrast needed for a working transistor. Ion implantation machines accelerate dopant ions and embed them in patterned regions of the wafer. One of the central process steps every chip goes through.
plain: Sprinkling specific atoms into silicon to change how it conducts electricity — a key step in building any transistor.

snappy: The basic multiplication operation between two vectors — multiply pairs of elements and sum.
detail: (1, 2, 3) · (4, 5, 6) = 1×4 + 2×5 + 3×6 = 32. Dot products measure similarity: vectors pointing the same direction have large positive dot products, opposite directions are negative. Every attention operation and embedding similarity computation in modern AI is built from dot products. The operation modern GPU tensor cores are built to maximise.
plain: A simple way to multiply two lists of numbers together: pair them up, multiply each pair, then add the results.

snappy: Counterintuitive phenomenon: a model's test error decreases, then increases, then decreases again as you scale up.
detail: Classical statistics predicts a single bias-variance trade-off curve, but very large modern models do something different — they keep improving long past the classical "overfitting" point. The second descent is a key reason gigantic models can be trained on relatively small data without disaster. Documented systematically by Belkin and others around 2018-2019.
plain: A strange pattern where a model gets worse as you make it bigger, then suddenly starts improving again past a certain size.

snappy: Simpler alternative to RLHF that skips the explicit reward model — just adjusts the model directly from preference data.
detail: RLHF is complex: train reward model, then run reinforcement learning on top. DPO collapses this into a single supervised loss that pushes the model toward preferred responses and away from rejected ones. Released by Stanford in 2023 and quickly adopted across the industry — Mistral, Meta, and many open-source projects use DPO instead of full RLHF. Often gets comparable results with much less engineering complexity.
plain: A simpler alternative to RLHF that teaches a model from preferred-versus-rejected example pairs in a single training step.

snappy: DeepMind's 2013 breakthrough that combined Q-learning with deep neural networks — solved Atari games from pixels.
detail: Used a CNN to estimate Q-values from raw screen pixels. Key innovations: experience replay (store transitions, sample randomly), target network (slowly-updated copy of the Q-network for training stability). Played 49 Atari games at or above human level. Kicked off the modern deep-RL era.
plain: DeepMind's 2013 breakthrough that learned to play Atari games straight from the pixels on screen.

snappy: The standard form of main memory — fast, dense, but loses its contents when power cuts.
detail: Every computer's RAM is DRAM. "Dynamic" because each bit is stored as a tiny charge that has to be refreshed every few milliseconds. HBM, GDDR, and LPDDR are all forms of DRAM optimised for different use cases. DRAM is one of the few major chip categories still produced at massive scale by just a handful of suppliers (Samsung, SK Hynix, Micron).
plain: The standard fast memory inside every computer — quick to read and write, but everything vanishes when the power cuts.

snappy: Using AI to identify, design, and optimise drug candidates faster than traditional methods.
detail: Spans target identification, virtual screening, molecule generation, ADMET prediction, and clinical-trial design. Companies: Recursion, Insilico Medicine, BenevolentAI, Isomorphic Labs, Insitro, Atomwise. AlphaFold-class structure prediction is a backbone tool. Most cited estimate: 5-10× reduction in early-stage discovery time when AI is integrated well.
plain: Using AI to find, design, and refine new drug candidates faster than traditional lab work allows.

snappy: Earlier-generation lithography using 193nm wavelength light — used for older process nodes and most non-leading-edge production.
detail: DUV machines from ASML, Nikon, and Canon are still the workhorses of most chip manufacturing. Chinese fabs (notably SMIC) have demonstrated production of 7nm-class chips using DUV with multi-pass patterning, although less efficiently than with EUV. China's ability to push DUV further is one of the more contested questions in chip-supply geopolitics.
plain: An older chip-printing technology that uses deep-ultraviolet light — still the workhorse for most chips that aren't bleeding edge.

snappy: DRAM with extra bits that let it detect and fix bit-flips — required for any serious server.
detail: Cosmic rays and electrical noise occasionally flip a bit in memory. Without ECC, that means a random crash, a corrupted result, or worse — bad gradient in training. Server-grade DRAM, HBM, and most modern data centre storage all use some form of ECC. Frontier AI training requires it because a single bad bit can poison an entire run.
plain: Special memory with extra bits that can spot and fix the random bit-flips caused by cosmic rays or electrical noise.

snappy: Software used to design, simulate, and verify chips — Synopsys, Cadence, and Siemens EDA dominate.
detail: Modern chip design is impossible without EDA. RTL synthesis turns code (Verilog, VHDL) into gates; place-and-route arranges gates physically; timing analysis verifies the chip will work at target speeds. The EDA industry is a small handful of huge companies; their tools are export-controlled and licence-restricted.
plain: Specialist software used to design, simulate, and double-check chips before they're sent to be manufactured.

snappy: Running compute close to users or devices instead of in centralised data centers — for low latency or local data sovereignty.
detail: AI inference on phones, cars, drones, factory floors, retail. Trades off model capability (smaller models fit on smaller hardware) against latency and privacy. Apple Intelligence's on-device 3B model is a frontier example. Edge AI cuts cloud cost and dependency, supports offline use, and improves response latency.
plain: Running computation on the device near the user — phones, cars, factory machines — instead of sending everything to a faraway server.

snappy: Quintillion (10¹⁸) math operations per second — the scale of modern frontier training infrastructure.
detail: 1 EFLOPS = 1,000 PFLOPS. Frontier model training runs at multi-EFLOPS aggregate compute. NVIDIA's GB200 NVL72 rack is rated at roughly 1.4 EFLOPS at FP8. The largest training clusters announced (xAI's Colossus, Meta's training infrastructure, Microsoft/OpenAI's Stargate) reach 10+ EFLOPS.
plain: A quintillion maths operations per second — the eye-watering scale at which today's biggest AI models are trained.

snappy: Special scalar associated with a square matrix — the amount by which the matrix stretches certain directions.
detail: If multiplying a matrix by a particular vector just rescales it (no rotation), that vector is an eigenvector and the scaling factor is its eigenvalue. Used throughout ML: PCA finds eigenvectors of covariance matrices; spectral methods analyse network behavior; stable training requires controlling eigenvalues of certain Jacobians.
plain: A single number that captures how much a matrix stretches certain special directions when you multiply by it.

snappy: Pairwise-comparison rating system originally from chess — used to rank LLMs on Chatbot Arena.
detail: Every win/loss between two models nudges their ratings in opposite directions. Higher Elo means the model wins more often head-to-head. The system is robust to selection bias in matchups but assumes preferences are transitive (if A beats B and B beats C, A tends to beat C).
plain: A scoring system borrowed from chess that ranks players — or chatbots — by who tends to win head-to-head matchups.

snappy: A learned numerical representation of a piece of data — text, image, audio — as a list of numbers.
detail: Embeddings let you measure similarity between very different inputs: "king" and "queen" have similar embeddings; an image of a dog and the word "dog" can also if trained jointly (CLIP). Foundational primitive for search, recommendation, classification, and clustering. OpenAI's text-embedding-3-large produces 3,072-dimensional vectors; Anthropic's Voyage embeddings are similar.
plain: A list of numbers that captures the meaning of a word, image, or sound so a computer can compare it to other things.

snappy: Research direction: AI that learns through interaction with the physical world rather than just reading text.
detail: Combines reinforcement learning, robotics, simulation, and increasingly vision-language models. The hope: physical-world experience grounds AI in ways pure text training can't. Tied closely to the humanoid-robot wave and the broader question of what "intelligence" means when separated from a body.
plain: AI that learns by interacting with the physical world — through a robot body, sensors, and real-world feedback — not just by reading.

snappy: Capabilities that appear suddenly above a certain model size — performance is near-zero, then jumps to useful.
detail: Heavily discussed since 2022. Examples: GPT-3 unlocked few-shot learning; GPT-4 unlocked many professional-exam capabilities. Whether emergence is "real" or an artefact of how metrics are measured remains debated — some apparent jumps disappear under continuous evaluation. Regardless, the unpredictability of when capabilities arrive is a major source of safety concern.
plain: Skills that suddenly appear once a model crosses a certain size threshold — useless small, useful large, with little warning in between.

snappy: The part of a model that reads the whole input upfront and prepares it for further processing.
detail: Encoders work bidirectionally — every word can see every other word — making them well-suited to understanding tasks like classification and search. BERT, Google's 2018 model that became the foundation for search ranking, is encoder-only. In encoder-decoder models like T5 or the original Transformer, the encoder digests the input before handing off to a decoder that writes the output.
plain: The part of a model that reads the entire input up front and turns it into something the rest of the model can work with.

snappy: Two-part design where one network reads the input and another writes the output.
detail: The original 2017 Transformer was encoder-decoder, built for translation. Modern translation models, summarisers, and speech recognisers (Whisper from OpenAI) still use this shape because the input-to-output mapping is clear. Decoder-only models have taken over chat and writing assistants, where the boundary between reading and writing is blurrier.
plain: A two-stage design where one network reads the input and a second network writes the output.

snappy: Approach where a single neural network maps from raw camera input directly to driving commands (steering, throttle, brake).
detail: Pioneered by NVIDIA's PilotNet (2016) and pushed by Tesla. Contrasts with the traditional perception → planning → control pipeline where each stage is a separate component. The bet: a single network can learn the right intermediate representations from data, given enough miles. Now the dominant paradigm for vision-only AV development.
plain: An approach where a single network turns raw camera footage straight into steering, throttle, and brake decisions.

snappy: US Bureau of Industry and Security tool — companies on the list need a special license to receive US-origin technology.
detail: Used to restrict Huawei, SMIC, YMTC, and many other Chinese technology firms. Has been the main legal instrument for individual-company export controls. Listed companies can't easily buy US chips, software, or fab equipment, creating a major operational headache for affected firms.
plain: A US government blacklist — companies on it need special permission to buy American chips, software, or equipment.

snappy: Information-theoretic measure of uncertainty — how surprising the outcome of a random process is.
detail: Defined as the average negative log probability. Used everywhere in ML: cross-entropy loss in classification, KL divergence in RLHF, maximum-entropy RL, decoding strategies. Higher entropy means more uncertainty; lower entropy means the outcome is more predictable. Foundational concept from Claude Shannon's 1948 paper.
plain: A measure of how uncertain or surprising the outcome of a random process is.

snappy: The world the RL agent acts in — provides states the agent observes and changes in response to actions.
detail: Could be a chess board, a video game, a simulated robot, a real robot, a stock market, or a dialogue with a human. The environment defines what observations the agent gets, what actions are available, and how rewards are computed. Designing a good environment is half the battle in RL research.
plain: The world an agent acts in — a game, simulation, or real-world setting that gives it observations and reacts to its choices.

snappy: One full pass through the training dataset — sometimes models train for many, sometimes less than one.
detail: If your dataset has 1 million examples, one epoch means showing the model all 1 million once. Image models traditionally trained for 100+ epochs. Modern LLMs, with datasets in the trillions of tokens, often train for less than one epoch — they see most of the data only once. The shift came as both data and model size scaled up: with enough data, you don't need to revisit it.
plain: One complete trip through all the training examples — some models do hundreds, modern giant ones often do less than one.

snappy: Simple exploration rule: take the best-looking action most of the time, but with probability epsilon, take a random one.
detail: Ubiquitous in early deep RL (DQN, Q-learning experiments). Epsilon typically anneals from 1.0 down to 0.01 over training. Crude but works surprisingly well in many environments. More sophisticated exploration strategies (curiosity, count-based, ensemble disagreement) help in harder environments.
plain: A simple exploration rule: usually pick what looks best, but occasionally roll the dice and try something random.

snappy: Meta's family of protein language models — open-weight, used widely in computational biology.
detail: ESM-1, ESM-2 (up to 15B parameters, 2022), ESM-3 (open as ESM Open, 2024). Used as backbone for many downstream protein-prediction tools. The 2024 ESM-3 launched alongside EvolutionaryScale, a Meta spinoff focused on biology applications. A pillar of the open biology-AI ecosystem alongside AlphaFold's open versions.
plain: A family of open AI models from Meta trained on protein sequences, used widely in computational biology research.
An AI chip designed to run only one type of model (the transformer) but to run it many times faster than general-purpose GPUs.
snappy: Specialised transformer-only ASIC from startup Etched — sacrifices flexibility for far-higher inference throughput on the dominant model family.
detail: Sohu bakes the transformer dataflow directly into silicon: no general-purpose programmability, no support for other architectures. Trade-off is dramatic per-watt inference throughput on transformer LLMs — Etched claims an order of magnitude versus contemporary H100/B200. Risky bet that the transformer remains the dominant frontier architecture for the chip's lifetime; pays off massively if it does. Early customers include several inference-focused startups.

snappy: Process step that removes silicon, metal, or oxide from a wafer after lithography exposes which regions to remove.
detail: Two main forms: wet etching (chemical bath) for less precise removal, dry etching (plasma) for precise patterning. Modern leading-edge chips use plasma etching for nearly every layer. Lam Research and Applied Materials make most of the world's etching equipment.
plain: A chipmaking step that chemically or with plasma removes the layers of silicon or metal you don't want to keep.

snappy: The universal networking standard — now scaling fast enough to compete with InfiniBand for AI.
detail: 400 Gigabit Ethernet is current; 800 GbE is rolling out in 2024-2025; 1.6 TbE is on the roadmap. Cheaper and more ubiquitous than InfiniBand. The Ultra Ethernet Consortium (UEC) is developing AI-specific extensions that aim to match InfiniBand's predictable latency for training workloads.
plain: The standard cabling tech that connects almost every computer to a network, now fast enough to wire up AI training clusters.

snappy: European Union regulation of AI systems, in force from 2024 with rolling provisions through 2027.
detail: Risk-based framework: bans some uses (social scoring, predictive policing), tightly regulates "high-risk" applications (hiring, credit, education), and imposes transparency rules on general-purpose AI. Frontier models (over 10²⁵ FLOPs of training compute) face additional safety, copyright, and reporting obligations. First major comprehensive AI law from a major jurisdiction.
plain: Europe's law setting rules for AI systems, with stricter requirements for high-risk uses like hiring, credit, and policing.

snappy: Light source at 13.5 nanometre wavelength — required for printing modern chip features below ~7nm.
detail: EUV is exclusively made by ASML. Each machine costs $200-400M+, weighs 180 tonnes, and uses tin droplets blasted with high-power lasers to generate the EUV light. Without EUV, modern chips don't exist. Subject to export controls preventing sale to China since 2019. ASML's EUV monopoly makes it one of the most geopolitically important companies in the world.
plain: An ultra-short wavelength of light used to print the tiniest features on modern chips — only one company in the world makes the machines.

snappy: When test-set questions accidentally appear in a model's training data — inflating reported scores.
detail: Widespread because benchmarks are public and models train on web scrapes that include the benchmarks themselves. A model that scores well on MMLU might have seen many of the questions in pretraining. Mitigation: hold-out new test sets, decontamination tools that check for overlap, private benchmarks unavailable to model trainers.
plain: When a test ends up inside the training data — the model has effectively seen the answer key, so its score is inflated.

snappy: Strictest scoring rule — the model's answer must match the reference character-for-character.
detail: Used in question answering and math benchmarks where there's a single correct answer. Punishes irrelevant differences (different spacing, units, capitalisation), so often paired with a normalization step. A model that says "42 apples" when the reference is "42" scores zero under naive exact match.
plain: A strict grading rule where the answer counts only if it matches the reference word-for-word, character-for-character.
The newest version of ASML's giant chip-printing machine, used to print patterns small enough for the next generation of chips.
snappy: ASML's latest production High-NA EUV lithography scanner, qualifying at imec in 2026 for sub-2nm chip-making.
detail: The EXE:5200 is the second-generation High-NA EUV system from ASML, with higher wafer-per-hour rate than the original EXE:5000 and refined optics. Imec's 2026 qualification milestone unblocks Intel 14A and TSMC A14 process integration, both of which depend on High-NA for their most critical mask levels. Each scanner sells for north of $380M, weighs about 165 tonnes, and ships in dozens of crates.

snappy: Risk that AI development could lead to human extinction or permanent loss of human autonomy.
detail: Central concern of the AI safety community. Sources of x-risk include misaligned superintelligence, AI-enabled biothreats, totalitarian misuse, and accidental cascading failures. Frontier labs publish responsible scaling policies that commit to pausing or restricting development if specific dangerous capabilities emerge. Public-facing debate is contested; "AI doomers" vs "e/acc" is the well-known shorthand.
plain: The worry that advanced AI could one day cause human extinction or permanently strip humanity of its freedom to choose.

snappy: The ability to provide human-understandable reasons for why an AI made a particular decision — distinct from interpretability research.
detail: Explainability targets end users and regulators: "Why was my loan denied?" Methods include SHAP values, LIME, attention visualisations, and natural-language rationales generated by the model itself. Interpretability is the deeper research field (mechanistic interpretability, sparse autoencoders) that aims to understand what's actually happening inside the network. The EU AI Act mandates "explainability" for high-risk systems, though what that means in practice for LLMs is unresolved.
plain: Being able to tell a person why an AI made a particular decision — important when a loan, hire, or diagnosis is on the line.

snappy: Fundamental trade-off in RL — should the agent try new things, or stick with what already works?
detail: Pure exploitation can get stuck in local optima. Pure exploration learns slowly and never collects much reward. Modern algorithms balance the two via various tricks: epsilon-greedy action selection, entropy bonuses, intrinsic curiosity rewards, count-based exploration. A central design choice in any RL system.
plain: The trade-off between trying new things to learn more, versus sticking with what already works to score the most points.

snappy: US restrictions on which AI-related products (chips, software, lithography equipment) can be sold to which countries.
detail: Major rounds in October 2022, October 2023, and updates through 2024-2025. Restricts NVIDIA's most advanced GPUs to China (forcing NVIDIA to make special restricted variants like the H800, then H20). Also restricts ASML EUV machines, certain chip design software. A central geopolitical lever in the US-China technology rivalry.
plain: US rules limiting which AI chips and chipmaking machines can be sold to which countries, mainly aimed at China.

snappy: Combines precision (how much of the answer is right?) and recall (how much of the right answer is covered?) into one number.
detail: Computed as the harmonic mean of precision and recall. Common for QA tasks where partial-credit makes sense — extractive question answering, named-entity recognition, span prediction. Less common for modern chat-style evals where outputs are full sentences rather than spans.
plain: A single number that combines two things — did the model get the right stuff, and how much of the right stuff did it find.

snappy: Factory that manufactures semiconductors — multi-billion-dollar buildings full of vacuum chambers, lithography machines, and ultra-clean rooms.
detail: A leading-edge fab costs $20-30B to build and another $10B+ to equip. TSMC operates the most advanced. Other major leading-edge fabs are Samsung (Korea), Intel (US), SMIC (China). Fab capacity is the binding physical constraint on the AI compute supply chain — TSMC is currently fully booked for the most advanced nodes through 2026-2027.
plain: A multi-billion-dollar factory full of ultra-clean rooms where computer chips are physically made.

snappy: Whether an AI system treats different groups of people equitably — a key concern in deployment, especially in hiring, lending, and law enforcement.
detail: Multiple competing definitions: demographic parity (equal outcomes across groups), equalised odds (equal error rates), individual fairness (similar people get similar outcomes). These often conflict mathematically — you can't satisfy all simultaneously. Notorious failures include Amazon's resume screener that downgraded women's CVs, and facial recognition systems with higher error rates for darker-skinned faces. Regulated by the EU AI Act and the proposed US AI Bill of Rights.
plain: Whether an AI system treats different groups of people equally, especially in high-stakes areas like hiring or lending.

snappy: A learned direction in a model's internal representation that corresponds to a recognisable concept.
detail: Features inside an LLM might include "the model is currently discussing Italy", "the user is asking about dates", "there's a Python `for` loop in the input". Found by sparse autoencoders and similar methods. Editing features can steer the model — Anthropic's "Golden Gate Claude" demo (2024) clamped one feature high and got an LLM that talked about the bridge incessantly.
plain: A pattern inside a model that lights up for a recognisable concept, like 'discussing Italy' or 'this is Python code'.

snappy: The art of crafting input features that make a model's job easier — pre-deep-learning, this was where most ML work happened.
detail: Date → day_of_week, age + height → BMI, location → census-tract demographics. Modern deep learning automates much of this, but feature engineering is still important for tabular ML, where domain expertise and clever features often beat raw model power.
plain: Hand-crafting helpful inputs for a model — turning a birth date into 'day of week' so the model has an easier time.

snappy: Training scheme where models train on data that stays on user devices — only weight updates are sent to the server.
detail: Google's Gboard keyboard learns from typing across many phones without uploading the text. Apple Intelligence uses similar techniques for on-device personalisation. Privacy-preserving alternative to centralised training. Limited by network bandwidth and device-side compute; useful for narrow scenarios more than frontier-scale training.
plain: Training a shared model on phones or laptops without the raw data ever leaving the device — only the lessons learned get sent back.

snappy: Giving a model a handful of examples in the prompt so it can pattern-match to the desired behaviour.
detail: Demonstrated by GPT-3 in 2020. Example: show the model 3-5 (question, answer) pairs, then ask a new question. The model often does much better than zero-shot. Modern instruction-tuned models need fewer examples (sometimes zero), but the technique is still useful for niche tasks and structured-output formats.
plain: Showing a model a handful of example question-and-answer pairs in the prompt so it copies the pattern for a new question.

snappy: Humanoid robot startup founded 2022 by Brett Adcock — among the highest-profile entrants in the humanoid race.
detail: Figure 01 (2023), Figure 02 (2024), Figure 03 (announced 2025). Initially partnered with OpenAI for vision-language reasoning; later moved to in-house models (Helix). Pilot deployments at BMW factories. Raised billions in funding through 2024-2025. Positioning: a general-purpose humanoid for industrial and eventually consumer settings.
plain: A high-profile startup building human-shaped robots, with early pilots inside BMW car factories.
