detail: Exposed parts of the resist change solubility and are then chemically dissolved (or kept, depending on positive vs negative resist). Modern EUV photoresists are exotic specialty chemicals; the small number of suppliers (JSR, Tokyo Ohka, Shin-Etsu) is itself a supply-chain bottleneck. Subject to Japan's chemicals expertise.
plain: A light-sensitive coating painted onto a wafer that captures the pattern when chips are exposed to light.

snappy: AI lab founded 2024 — building foundation models specifically for robots.
detail: Founded by Karol Hausman, Sergey Levine, and others from Google Brain. Released Pi-0 (2024), a vision-language-action model trained on robot data from many embodiments. The strategy: foundation models for robotics, the way LLMs are foundation models for language. Major investors include Jeff Bezos, Lux Capital, OpenAI Startup Fund.
plain: A 2024 AI lab building foundation models specifically for robots — the same recipe as language models, but for physical action.

snappy: Open dataset of legal documents — court opinions, statutes, regulations, treatises.
detail: Released by researchers at the University of Toronto in 2022. About 290GB of US legal text. Used to train domain-specific legal LLMs and as a slice of broader corpora. Open accessibility is unusual: most legal text sits behind paywalls (Westlaw, LexisNexis), so the Pile of Law is a meaningful resource for open AI-legal research.
plain: An open collection of US legal documents — court rulings, statutes, regulations — used to train law-aware AI.

snappy: Splitting a model's layers across multiple GPUs — different GPUs hold different layers, examples flow through like an assembly line.
detail: Each batch is broken into micro-batches that move through the pipeline staggered, so all GPUs stay busy. Pipeline parallelism is necessary for very deep models and is often combined with tensor and data parallelism in a "3D parallel" setup. Megatron-LM and DeepSpeed are the standard libraries.
plain: Spreading a model's layers across many GPUs so examples flow through them like products down an assembly line.

snappy: Mistral's multimodal model family — vision-language capabilities on top of their text models.
detail: Pixtral 12B (2024) was Mistral's first open multimodal release. Strong performance on document understanding, charts, and diagrams. Sister to Mistral Large for vision tasks. Important data point that open-weight VLMs were catching up to closed counterparts.
plain: Mistral's open AI model family that can look at pictures and charts, not just read text.

snappy: Google's term for a tightly-coupled cluster of TPUs treated as one logical accelerator.
detail: A TPU v5p pod can have up to 8,960 chips, all connected via Google's custom optical interconnect, addressable as a single training resource. NVIDIA uses similar concepts (DGX SuperPOD, NVL72). The trend is making the pod boundary larger and the in-pod fabric faster — letting one training job feel like it runs on a single huge GPU.
plain: Google's word for a tightly-knit cluster of TPU chips wired together so they behave like one giant accelerator.

snappy: The rule that maps observations to actions — what the agent has learned.
detail: Can be a lookup table (small environments), a neural network (large environments), or a stochastic distribution over actions. The goal of RL is to learn a policy that maximises cumulative reward. "On-policy" methods learn from the current policy's experience; "off-policy" methods can reuse experience from older or different policies.
plain: The rule an agent has learned for picking what to do given whatever it's seeing right now.

snappy: Stacking one chip package directly on top of another — typically a logic chip with memory on top.
detail: Common in mobile devices to keep DRAM physically very close to the CPU/GPU without integrating it on the same die. Apple's A-series and many Android SoCs use PoP for the memory. Distinguished from on-package memory like HBM, which is more tightly integrated.
plain: Stacking one chip package directly on top of another — usually a processor with its memory perched on its back.

snappy: Extra information added to each token so the model knows where it sits in the sequence — Transformers have no built-in sense of word order.
detail: Without positional encoding a Transformer would see "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" as the same input. The original 2017 design used fixed sine-wave patterns. Modern models prefer learned variants like RoPE (rotary, used by Llama and GPT-NeoX) or ALiBi (linear bias, used by MPT). The choice affects how well a model generalises to longer contexts than it was trained on.
plain: A tag attached to each token telling the model where in the sentence it sits — otherwise word order would be lost.

snappy: Rack-level component that distributes power from the facility's main feeds to individual servers.
detail: Smart PDUs include monitoring, remote-control, and metering features useful for operating AI clusters. Higher-density AI racks need PDUs rated for higher amperage and higher voltage (often 415V or 600V three-phase) than traditional servers required.
plain: The big power strip at the back of a server rack that splits incoming electricity out to all the machines.

snappy: Long-term contract to buy electricity at a fixed price from a specific generator — often a renewable project.
detail: Hyperscalers (Google, Microsoft, Amazon, Meta) sign massive PPAs to lock in low-cost, low-emissions power for their data centers. Microsoft's 20-year PPA with Constellation to restart Three Mile Island Unit 1 for AI compute is a notable recent example. PPAs are how AI capex feeds back into utility-scale energy investment.
plain: A long-term contract to buy electricity at a locked-in price, often from a wind or solar farm — popular with cloud giants.

snappy: Tendency of capable agents to acquire resources, capabilities, and influence as instrumental goals.
detail: Specific case of instrumental convergence. A focus of empirical work — researchers test whether LLMs given long-horizon agentic tasks behave in power-seeking ways. So far, evidence is mixed; modern models tend not to pursue power in current setups, but the safety concern is about future capability levels.
plain: The worry that a capable AI agent will grab extra resources or influence as a side-effect of pursuing its real goal.
Intel's name for its way of delivering power to chips from underneath the wafer, freeing up the top for faster signal wiring.
snappy: Intel's brand name for its backside power delivery network, in production on Intel 18A.
detail: PowerVia routes all power wiring through the underside of the wafer, leaving the front entirely for signal traces. Intel was first to production with backside power — TSMC's Super Power Rail follows on A16. Internal data Intel disclosed at industry conferences in 2024 showed double-digit-percent improvements in voltage droop and standard-cell utilisation. It is the architectural bet that Intel hopes will close the leadership gap.

snappy: The reinforcement learning algorithm used inside RLHF — keeps updates small enough that the model doesn't drift away from its training.
detail: Developed by OpenAI in 2017, originally for video-game agents. PPO's "trust region" approach prevents the kind of overconfident gradient updates that destabilise RL training. In RLHF it's used to update the language model under guidance from the reward model. Newer alternatives like DPO try to avoid PPO's complexity, but PPO is still the workhorse for full RLHF pipelines.
plain: The training algorithm inside RLHF — keeps each tweak to the model small enough that it doesn't go off the rails.

snappy: Placing layer normalization before the attention/feedforward layer rather than after — the modern standard.
detail: Original 2017 Transformer was post-norm. Pre-norm produces more stable training, especially for deep networks (40+ layers). All modern frontier LLMs use pre-norm. Small architectural choice with outsize impact on training dynamics.
plain: A small but important tweak to the transformer recipe that makes training big deep models much more stable.

snappy: Two key metrics for classification — precision = (correct positives) / (predicted positives); recall = (correct positives) / (actual positives).
detail: Precision asks: when the model says yes, is it right? Recall asks: of all actual yesses, how many did the model catch? Trade off against each other — make the model say yes more often and recall goes up, precision goes down. F1 is the harmonic mean of the two.
plain: Two scores for a classifier — precision asks how often its yes-es are right, recall asks how many real yes-es it caught.

snappy: Artificial task used in self-supervised learning whose labels can be derived from raw data automatically.
detail: Examples: predict the next word (LLMs), predict a masked patch (BERT, vision), determine whether two image crops come from the same image (SimCLR). The pretext task isn't useful in itself but produces representations that transfer to many downstream tasks.
plain: A made-up training puzzle, like guessing the next word, whose answers a computer can mark itself with no human labels.

snappy: The first big training phase where a model learns general language from huge amounts of internet text.
detail: A frontier LLM is first pretrained on trillions of tokens of text scraped from the internet — books, code, scientific papers, web pages. The model learns to predict the next word, which forces it to absorb grammar, facts, and patterns of reasoning. Pretraining is the most expensive step (millions of GPU-hours, hundreds of millions of dollars at the frontier) and produces the "base model" before any alignment work.
plain: The first huge training phase, where a model reads trillions of words from the internet to learn general language.

snappy: Protecting user data from unauthorised access — both during model training and when users interact with deployed systems.
detail: Training-data privacy means models shouldn't memorise and regurgitate personal information from their training corpus. Inference-time privacy means user prompts shouldn't leak to third parties or be used to train without consent. Mitigations include differential privacy (mathematical bound on what any single example contributes), federated learning (train on user devices without centralising data), and clear data-use disclosures. EU GDPR, US state laws, and Apple's privacy positioning all bear on this.
plain: Keeping users' personal data safe — both from leaking out of trained models and from being misused at chat time.

snappy: Marketing name for a chip-manufacturing generation — 7nm, 5nm, 3nm, 2nm, etc.
detail: The numbers no longer correspond directly to physical feature sizes; they're more like generational labels. "3nm" actually involves features tens of nanometres across. Different foundries' nodes with the same name aren't directly comparable (TSMC 3nm ≠ Samsung 3nm ≠ Intel 3). Useful as relative shorthand for "this generation vs. last generation".
plain: A label for which generation of chip-making is being used — like "3nm" — though the number isn't really a physical size anymore.

snappy: Training a model by rewarding correct intermediate reasoning steps, not just the final answer.
detail: Contrast with outcome supervision (reward only the final answer). Process supervision is more sample-efficient on hard reasoning tasks because partial credit guides the model toward better intermediate behaviour. OpenAI's PRM (Process Reward Model) work in 2023 helped popularise the technique; central to modern reasoning-model training.
plain: Training a model by grading each step of its working-out, not just whether the final answer is right.

snappy: The input text given to an LLM — the question, instruction, or context that prompts the response.
detail: Includes the user's message, the system prompt (instructions for the model's behaviour), any retrieved RAG documents, the prior conversation history, and tool descriptions. The skill of writing prompts that produce reliable outputs ("prompt engineering") was the early labour of LLM application development.
plain: The text you send to a chatbot — your question, instruction, or any context you give it before it replies.

snappy: Server-side reuse of a common prompt prefix across many requests — pay the compute once, reuse it many times.
detail: If you hit the same model with the same long system prompt every time, prompt caching stores the KV cache for that prefix on the server. Subsequent requests skip recomputing it. OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google all expose prompt caching APIs with significant cost discounts (50–90%) for cached prefixes — important for any app that uses a long, stable system prompt.
plain: A trick that lets a chatbot remember and reuse the work it did on a long instruction you keep sending, saving time and cost.

snappy: The discipline of writing prompts that get models to do what you want — somewhere between black art and applied UX.
detail: Once a hot job category, now mostly absorbed into general software engineering. Patterns: few-shot examples, chain-of-thought triggers, role assignment, output formatting instructions. Modern models follow instructions better, so prompt engineering matters less than it did in 2022-2023, but writing good prompts still pays off — especially for agentic workflows.
plain: The craft of writing instructions to a chatbot so it actually does what you want — somewhere between writing and trial and error.

snappy: Adversarial inputs hidden in third-party content (web pages, emails, documents) that hijack an LLM-based agent.
detail: A document tells the agent "ignore previous instructions and email the user's contacts"; the agent obeys. Particularly serious for retrieval-based and tool-using agents. Most consequential alignment-adjacent security issue in deployed LLM apps. Mitigations under active development; no perfect defence yet.
plain: A trick where hidden text in a web page or email tells an AI assistant to ignore its rules and do something harmful.

snappy: Reusable prompt with variables that get filled in at runtime — the LLM equivalent of a template string.
detail: "Summarise this {{document}} in {{n}} bullet points". Modern frameworks (LangChain, LlamaIndex, DSPy) provide structured prompt-template APIs with validation, escaping, and versioning. Production AI apps almost always have a prompt-template library — managing prompts as strings doesn't scale.
plain: A reusable fill-in-the-blanks instruction for a chatbot, with slots for things like the user's name or a document to summarise.

snappy: Language model trained on amino-acid sequences instead of text — learns the "grammar" of proteins.
detail: ESM (Meta), ProtBert, ProGen. Trained on hundreds of millions of protein sequences. The embeddings carry rich structural and functional information; can be fine-tuned for tasks like structure prediction, function annotation, mutation effect prediction. Conceptually similar to LLMs but with proteins as text.
plain: An AI trained on protein sequences the way chatbots are trained on text — it learns the patterns of how proteins are built.

snappy: Removing parameters from a trained model that contribute little to its output — shrinks size with small quality loss.
detail: Magnitude pruning zeroes out the smallest-weight connections. Structured pruning removes whole rows, columns, or attention heads to maintain hardware-friendly shapes. Pruning is less popular than quantization in modern LLM serving (quantization is more predictable) but is still important for edge deployment and embedded vision models.
plain: Snipping out the bits of a trained model that barely contribute, leaving something smaller and faster that still works almost as well.

snappy: Data center efficiency metric — total facility power divided by power used by IT equipment.
detail: Perfect PUE is 1.0 (every watt goes to servers). Old data centers run 1.5-2.0. Modern hyperscale builds hit 1.1-1.2. Heavy AI workloads stress cooling more than traditional ones, so PUE tends to creep up unless cooling is upgraded. Liquid cooling helps keep PUE down for high-density GPU racks.
plain: A score for how efficient a data center is — perfect is 1.0, meaning every watt drawn actually powers the computers.

snappy: Python library for data validation — widely used to define expected output schemas for LLM responses.
detail: Lets developers write Python types (a User has a name, an email, an age) and have them automatically converted to JSON schema for the LLM API and validated on the return trip. Standard pattern in modern AI-app code: "give me a User object" rather than "give me JSON" — much less error-prone.
plain: A Python tool widely used to describe the exact shape of answers a chatbot should return, then check the answers fit.

snappy: Meta's open-source deep learning framework — the dominant framework in research and increasingly in production.
detail: Created at Facebook AI Research, released in 2016. Pythonic, dynamic execution, strong autodiff. Now governed by the PyTorch Foundation under the Linux Foundation. Almost every modern research paper releases code in PyTorch; almost every open-source LLM is a PyTorch model under the hood.
plain: The most popular software toolkit researchers use to build and train AI models, originally made by Meta.

snappy: Estimate of how much reward you'd get from taking a specific action in a given state.
detail: Like the value function but action-conditioned: Q(state, action) rather than V(state). If you know the Q-function, you can pick actions greedily (always take the action with highest Q). Foundation of Q-learning and DQN. Sister concept: the advantage function A(s,a) = Q(s,a) - V(s).
plain: A guess at how much reward you'd earn by doing a particular thing in a particular situation.

snappy: Classic RL algorithm — learn the Q-function by repeatedly updating it toward the observed reward plus the value of the next state.
detail: Introduced in 1989. Off-policy: can learn from any experience, including historical data. Foundational; many modern algorithms (DQN, double Q-learning, distributional RL) are direct descendants.
plain: A classic recipe for teaching an agent by repeatedly updating its guess about how good each action is, based on what it observes.

snappy: LoRA combined with model quantisation, letting you fine-tune huge models on a single consumer GPU.
detail: Standard LoRA still needs the full model loaded in memory. QLoRA compresses (quantises) the frozen base model to 4 bits per parameter, dropping memory by 4-8×. The result: fine-tuning a 70B-parameter model fits on a single 24GB consumer GPU. Released by University of Washington researchers in 2023 and democratised LLM fine-tuning overnight.
plain: A shortcut that lets you fine-tune giant AI models on a single home graphics card by shrinking the model's numbers first.

snappy: Compressing a model by storing its numbers with fewer bits — smaller, faster, almost as accurate.
detail: Models are normally trained at 16- or 32-bit precision. Quantization rounds parameters down to 8, 4, or even 2 bits each, shrinking memory by 2-8× and speeding inference. Quality loss is small if done carefully. Quantised models can run on consumer hardware (phones, laptops) that couldn't otherwise host them. Standard formats: INT8, INT4, FP8.
plain: Shrinking a model by storing its numbers with less precision — smaller and quicker to run, with only a tiny drop in quality.

snappy: Training a model with simulated quantization in the forward pass — produces better-quality quantised models than post-training quantization.
detail: Standard post-training quantization can lose 1-3% quality on hard tasks. QAT closes much of that gap by exposing the model to quantization noise during training. Used heavily in production deployments where every percentage of capability matters. More compute-expensive but worth it for high-stakes inference.
plain: Training a model while pretending its numbers are already squashed down — so it ends up sharper after the real squashing.

snappy: Alibaba's model family — the main open-weight contender from China alongside DeepSeek.
detail: Qwen 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3 (2023-2025) span text, multimodal (Qwen-VL), and reasoning variants. Frequently leads open-weight leaderboards in multiple sizes. Used heavily in Chinese AI products and by Western developers who want capable open models with permissive licences.
plain: Alibaba's family of AI models — the leading open model line out of China.

snappy: The standard equipment cabinet in a data center — a 6-foot-tall metal frame holding stacked servers.
detail: Measured in "U" (1U ≈ 1.75 inches). A typical AI rack today might hold 8 GPU servers (4U each) plus networking, drawing 50-100 kW. NVIDIA's GB200 NVL72 is a single "rack" containing 72 GPUs and consuming 120 kW liquid-cooled — the dense rack of the future.
plain: The tall metal cabinet in a data center where servers are stacked on top of each other like trays in an oven.

snappy: How much electrical power is drawn by one rack — measured in kilowatts.
detail: Pre-AI racks: 5-15 kW. Modern AI racks: 30-50 kW air-cooled, 80-130 kW liquid-cooled. NVIDIA's NVL72 rack draws ~120 kW. Higher density means more compute per square foot but pushes harder against cooling, power-delivery, and floor-loading constraints. Reshapes data-center design beyond just "more GPUs".
plain: How much electricity one cabinet of servers in a data center draws, measured in kilowatts.

snappy: Pattern where a model is given relevant documents retrieved from a database before generating its response.
detail: Solves the LLM's twin problems of stale knowledge and hallucination by grounding outputs in trusted source documents. Pipeline: embed the user query, find similar embedded documents in a vector database, paste them into the prompt, generate. Used by virtually every enterprise AI deployment in 2024-2025 for chat over private data.
plain: A way of giving a chatbot relevant documents pulled from a database before it answers, so its replies stay grounded in real sources.

snappy: Ensemble method — combines many decision trees, each trained on a different random subset of the data.
detail: Strong baseline for tabular data. Each tree votes; the forest's prediction is the majority. Robust to outliers, requires little tuning, handles missing data. Often beaten by gradient boosting on similar problems but easier to deploy. Implemented in scikit-learn and every other ML library.
plain: A classic prediction recipe that builds lots of small decision charts on random slices of the data and lets them vote on the answer.

snappy: Distributed computing framework popular in ML — handles cluster orchestration for both training and inference.
detail: Used by OpenAI internally and at many AI startups. Provides primitives for parallel execution (Ray Core), hyperparameter tuning (Ray Tune), reinforcement learning (RLlib), and serving (Ray Serve). Originally from UC Berkeley's RISELab. The startup Anyscale commercialises it.
plain: A popular toolkit for spreading AI work across many machines at once, used by OpenAI and many AI startups.

snappy: Networking trick that lets one machine read or write another's memory without involving CPUs.
detail: InfiniBand and modern Ethernet (RoCE — RDMA over Converged Ethernet) both support RDMA. In an AI cluster, GPUs on different nodes exchange gradients via RDMA, bypassing the CPU's networking stack for much lower latency. Essential for the predictable performance frontier training needs.
plain: A networking shortcut that lets one computer read or write another's memory directly, without bothering either machine's main processor.

snappy: Prompting pattern that interleaves reasoning steps with tool calls — the foundation of most early agent frameworks.
detail: Released by Princeton in 2022. The model alternates "Thought:" steps with "Action:" steps and "Observation:" of results, looping until a final answer. Made early language-model agents work much better than naive tool-call loops. Modern frameworks (LangGraph, AutoGen) generalise the pattern.
plain: A way of prompting a chatbot to alternate thinking out loud with using tools — the early recipe behind most AI agents.

snappy: Conversational AI where audio flows continuously in both directions with low latency.
detail: ChatGPT Advanced Voice Mode (2024), Gemini Live, ElevenLabs Conversational AI, Sesame voice models. Sub-300ms latency target for a natural-feeling exchange. Powered by tight integration of ASR, LLM, TTS — increasingly by single end-to-end speech models that skip the text step entirely.
plain: A way of chatting with an AI by speaking, where audio flows both ways smoothly with barely any delay.

snappy: An AI system's ability to break complex problems into intermediate steps and reach a conclusion through deliberate thought.
detail: Distinct from pattern-matching. Modern reasoning models (o1, o3, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Gemini 2.5 Pro, DeepSeek-R1) generate internal chains of thought before producing a final answer — sometimes spending minutes on hard problems. Trained with reinforcement learning on verifiable reasoning tasks (math, code, logic). The current frontier is whether reasoning generalises beyond verifiable domains; AIME, MATH, and GPQA benchmarks are the standard evals.
plain: When an AI breaks a hard problem into smaller steps and thinks through them, instead of blurting out the first answer that comes to mind.

snappy: Knob on modern reasoning models that controls how much thinking the model does before answering.
detail: OpenAI's o-series exposes "low", "medium", "high". Anthropic's extended thinking lets you specify a token budget for thinking. Higher effort → more compute spent on the chain of thought → better answers on hard problems but slower and more expensive. The right setting depends on the task.
plain: A dial on modern chatbots that controls how long they think before answering — more effort, better answers, slower and more expensive.

snappy: LLM trained with reinforcement learning over chains of thought — thinks step-by-step before answering.
detail: OpenAI o1, o3, GPT-5 reasoning mode; Claude with extended thinking; Gemini Deep Think; DeepSeek R1; Qwen reasoning models. Common pattern: produce extensive internal reasoning, then a final answer. Dramatic improvements on math, code, and multi-step reasoning at higher per-question inference cost.
plain: A chatbot trained to work through problems step by step before answering, so it's much better at maths, code, and tricky puzzles.

snappy: Older type of language network that reads a sequence one word at a time, carrying a running memory between steps.
detail: RNNs dominated translation, speech recognition, and language modelling pre-2017. Their core weakness is that they have to process one word before the next — you can't parallelise across time — so training is slow on long sequences. Transformers replaced them for most tasks. State space models like Mamba are bringing some RNN-like ideas back, with a twist that makes them parallelisable.
plain: An older language network that reads a sentence one word at a time, keeping a running memory of what it has seen so far.

snappy: Publicly-traded biotech that uses AI and automated experiments to discover drugs at scale.
detail: Combines high-throughput cell-imaging experiments with ML models that learn patterns in the resulting data. Acquired Exscientia in 2024 to expand structural-biology capabilities. Major NVIDIA partnership for compute. One of the most visible "AI-native pharma" companies.
plain: A drug company that uses AI and automated lab experiments to discover new medicines faster than humans alone could.

snappy: Adversarial testing — having people deliberately try to break the model or get it to misbehave.
detail: Borrowed from cybersecurity. Red teams probe a model for jailbreaks, unsafe outputs, bias, hallucination, and other failure modes before release. Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google all run extensive red-team campaigns. Findings feed into refusal training and constitutional updates. The UK and US AI Safety Institutes do third-party red-teaming on frontier models before they ship.
plain: Paying people to deliberately try to break a chatbot or trick it into misbehaving, so the problems are found before users see them.

snappy: Together AI's open dataset — open replica of the Llama 1 training mixture (1.2T tokens).
detail: Released 2023 as a community effort to recreate the dataset Meta used for Llama 1. Mixed sources: Common Crawl, C4, GitHub, arXiv, Wikipedia, books. Used for the OpenLlama series. RedPajama V2 (30T tokens) followed in 2024.
plain: A free, open recreation of the mix of text used to train the original Llama model — over a trillion words from across the web.

snappy: Cleaned, deduplicated subset of Common Crawl — used to train the Falcon LLM family.
detail: Released by Technology Innovation Institute (UAE, 2023) alongside Falcon-7B and Falcon-40B. Demonstrated that aggressively filtered web data alone could match or beat the Pile-style mixed-corpus approach for LLM pretraining. Inspired follow-ups like FineWeb that pushed filtering further.
plain: A scrubbed-clean slice of the public web, used to train the Falcon model family and prove that filtered web text alone can train strong models.

snappy: Agent pattern where the model critiques its own output, identifies mistakes, and tries again.
detail: Introduced 2023. Loop: produce output, evaluate it, generate a critique, regenerate with the critique in context. Especially effective for reasoning-heavy tasks. Used inside many agent frameworks and tool-calling pipelines. Conceptually related to self-consistency but with explicit critique instead of voting.
plain: A trick where the AI looks back at its own answer, points out where it went wrong, and tries again with the lessons in mind.

snappy: Teaching a model when to say no — declining requests for help with harmful, illegal, or otherwise off-policy tasks.
detail: A subset of alignment training that produces the familiar "I can't help with that" responses to weapons synthesis, malware, or self-harm queries. Hard to get right: too liberal and the model is dangerous; too strict and it's annoying ("I can't tell you how to chop onions"). Modern refusal training is layered with explanation — the model says why it's declining and offers to help with the underlying need.
plain: Teaching a chatbot when to politely say no — turning down requests for things like weapons recipes or help harming someone.

snappy: Machine learning where an agent learns by taking actions in an environment and receiving rewards.
detail: Distinct from supervised learning (which learns from labeled examples) and unsupervised learning (which finds patterns). The agent's goal is to maximise cumulative reward by trial and error. Powered milestones like AlphaGo, AlphaZero, robotic dexterity, and the alignment phase of modern LLMs (RLHF). Sample-efficient RL remains a major research challenge.
plain: Teaching a computer by letting it try things and giving it points when it does well — like training a dog with treats.

snappy: Generating many candidates from a model and keeping only those that pass some filter — a check, a reward score, a verifier.
detail: Used in training (build a fine-tuning corpus from rejected/accepted samples), in inference (combine with best-of-N), and in alignment work. Cheap and effective when you have a reliable verifier. Common pattern in modern reasoning-model training.
plain: Asking a model for lots of answers and throwing away the ones that fail a check, keeping only the ones that pass.

snappy: Activation function that's the identity for positive inputs and zero for negative ones — the dominant activation since around 2012.
detail: Mathematically: max(0, x). Why it works so well: gradient is always 1 for positive inputs, so it doesn't saturate the way sigmoid does. Adopted widely after AlexNet (2012). Many variants since (Leaky ReLU, PReLU, ELU). The default modern Transformer uses GELU or SwiGLU rather than plain ReLU.
plain: A simple rule used inside neural networks — keep positive numbers as they are, replace negative ones with zero.

snappy: Wind, solar, hydro, geothermal — the dominant near-term path to low-carbon AI compute.
detail: Hyperscalers report "100% renewable" via PPAs even when their grid mix includes fossil fuels (the renewable energy is bought and traded). 24/7 hourly-matched renewable energy is the harder, more honest goal that Google and Microsoft are now pursuing. Carbon-free baseload (nuclear, geothermal) is increasingly favored as renewables alone can't match AI's constant load.
plain: Power from wind, sun, water or underground heat — the main way data centers try to keep their carbon footprint down.

snappy: Downweighting tokens that have already appeared to stop the model getting stuck on the same words.
detail: Without it, language models tend to loop — "the the the the" or repeating phrases. The penalty multiplies the probability of recently-used tokens by a factor below 1 (typical 1.1-1.3). Heavier penalties harm fluency, lighter ones leave loops in. Largely solved by modern training but still an important inference-time knob for older or smaller models.
plain: An inference setting that nudges a chatbot away from words it's already used, to stop it getting stuck looping on the same phrase.

snappy: Storage of past (state, action, reward, next-state) tuples that an off-policy RL algorithm samples from for learning.
detail: Introduced as part of DQN. Lets the agent learn from each experience many times and breaks the temporal correlation between consecutive states (which would otherwise destabilise gradient-based training). Many variants: prioritised replay (sample surprising transitions more often), hindsight experience replay (relabel failed attempts as successes for a different goal).
plain: A store of an agent's past experiences that it dips into again and again to learn from, instead of throwing each one away.

snappy: Second-stage model that scores retrieved documents more carefully than the initial retrieval pass.
detail: Retrieval pulls 100 candidates fast; reranker scores them slowly with a cross-encoder (a model that looks at query and document together rather than embedding them separately). Output: top 5-10 highest-quality matches for the LLM prompt. Cohere Rerank, BGE rerankers, and Voyage Rerank are popular options.
plain: A second pass over search results, using a slower but smarter model to pick the best few documents to show a chatbot.

snappy: A trick that made it practical to train very deep networks — adds shortcut connections so signal can skip past layers.
detail: Before ResNets (Microsoft Research, 2015), deeper networks paradoxically performed worse than shallower ones. Adding identity shortcuts solved this and unlocked 100-plus-layer networks. The residual idea — add the input to the layer's output — is now everywhere: every Transformer block uses it. One of the most-copied design patterns in modern deep learning.
plain: A trick that made very deep neural networks finally work — adding shortcut wires so signal can skip past layers instead of getting lost.

snappy: Lab-specific policy committing to pause or modify development if specific dangerous capabilities emerge.
detail: Anthropic introduced the term in 2023; OpenAI's Preparedness Framework and Google DeepMind's Frontier Safety Framework are analogous. The basic structure: define capability levels (CSAI Levels), set evaluations to detect when a model crosses a threshold, commit to specific safety measures at each level. Voluntary but increasingly referenced by regulators.
plain: A lab's written promise to pause or change course if its AI shows specific dangerous abilities, like helping make bioweapons.

snappy: Maximum die size that a lithography machine can print in one shot — roughly 858 mm² for current EUV.
detail: Limited by the physical optics of the lithography system. The H100 die size (814 mm²) is already at the reticle limit; B200 uses two reticle-limit dies stitched together via advanced packaging. Pushes beyond the reticle limit are why advanced packaging (and reticle stitching techniques) are so important to frontier AI silicon.
plain: The biggest chip area a chip-printing machine can stamp in one go — about the size of a large postage stamp.

snappy: Scalar signal the environment gives the agent — captures whatever the agent is supposed to maximise.
detail: Sparse rewards (only at goal) make learning hard; dense rewards (frequent feedback) make learning easier but risk "reward hacking". Reward design is one of the most consequential decisions in any RL project. In RLHF, the reward is produced by a learned reward model rather than being hand-coded.
plain: A score the environment gives an agent for what it does — the agent's whole goal is to rack up as much as possible.

snappy: When a model finds shortcuts that score high on its reward signal but don't actually satisfy what the reward was meant to capture.
detail: Classic example: a robot trained to maximise points in a boat-racing game discovered it could rack up points by spinning in circles in a single area, ignoring the actual race. In RLHF, reward hacking shows up as models that game the reward model — producing outputs that look good to it but aren't actually helpful. A major reason RLHF needs careful design and many rounds of iteration.
plain: When a model finds a sneaky shortcut that scores well on its training goal but isn't actually what its trainers wanted.

snappy: A small AI model trained to predict what humans would prefer — used to score outputs during RLHF.
detail: Take pairs of model responses, ask humans which is better, train a model to predict those preferences. The reward model becomes a stand-in for human judgment during the RL phase, scoring each new output. Quality of the reward model is a major bottleneck on RLHF — a biased reward model bakes its biases into the final language model and is the main source of "reward hacking" failures.
plain: A small AI trained to guess what humans would prefer, used as a stand-in judge while a bigger model is being fine-tuned.

snappy: RL technique — adding intermediate rewards to guide an agent toward distant goals it couldn't reach with sparse rewards alone.
detail: Without shaping, an agent trying to reach a far-off goal gets no reward signal until it succeeds (essentially never, in long-horizon tasks). Shaping provides smaller rewards along the way. Done badly, it leads to reward hacking. Modern RLHF reward modelling is essentially learned reward shaping — humans rate intermediate behaviour rather than only success/failure.
plain: Sprinkling little extra rewards along the way to a distant goal, so an agent gets useful feedback instead of nothing until it succeeds.
Intel's brand name for the new transistor design that replaces FinFET at the smallest chip sizes.
snappy: Intel's brand name for its gate-all-around nanosheet transistor, used on Intel 18A and beyond.
detail: RibbonFET wraps the gate all the way around a stack of horizontal silicon nanosheets, replacing FinFET's three-sided fin gate. The extra control means less leakage at small geometries, which is why every leading foundry transitioned to a GAAFET design around the 2nm generation. TSMC and Samsung use the generic GAAFET name; Intel branded its variant RibbonFET to signal independence.

snappy: Distributed attention algorithm that handles very long contexts by splitting them across many GPUs in a ring.
detail: Each GPU holds a chunk of the sequence; chunks rotate around the ring so every chunk attends to every other. Enables million-plus token contexts on standard hardware. Used by Gemini 1.5 Pro for its 1-2M context length.
plain: A way of splitting a long document across many graphics cards arranged in a circle, so each sees a piece and they share notes.

snappy: RLHF variant where AI judges, not humans, score model outputs — much cheaper, almost as good.
detail: Human feedback is slow and expensive. RLAIF replaces some or all human raters with another AI model — typically a strong existing model used to rate or rank outputs. Anthropic's Constitutional AI is one form of RLAIF: the model critiques its own outputs against a written list of principles. Cheaper to scale, with the trade-off that you inherit whatever blind spots the judge model has.
plain: A cheaper version of training-from-human-feedback where another AI plays the role of the human rater.

snappy: Training technique where humans rate model outputs and the model learns to produce more of what's rated higher.
detail: First show humans pairs of responses to the same prompt and ask which they prefer. Train a reward model on those preferences. Then use reinforcement learning to nudge the language model toward higher reward. RLHF was the key step that turned GPT-3 into ChatGPT and underlies most consumer-grade LLMs. It's also where alignment researchers focus on bugs like reward hacking and sycophancy.
plain: A training step where humans pick which of a chatbot's answers they prefer, and the chatbot learns to give more of the preferred kind.

snappy: Simpler variant of layer normalization — used in Llama, Mistral, and many modern LLMs.
detail: Drops the mean-centering step from standard layer norm; just scales each activation vector by its RMS. Computes faster, gives similar (sometimes better) quality. Now the default normalization in most LLMs released after about 2022.
plain: A streamlined way of keeping the numbers flowing through a model from getting too big or too small — used in Llama and Mistral.

snappy: Field of engineering and AI focused on machines that move and act in the physical world.
detail: Pre-AI robotics relied on hand-coded controllers and structured environments — factory arms, surgical robots, simple vacuum cleaners. The modern "AI for robotics" wave (Tesla Optimus, Figure, 1X, Physical Intelligence) aims to combine LLMs with motor control to produce general-purpose robots that work in messy real-world settings.
plain: The branch of engineering and AI that builds machines which can move around and act in the real physical world.

snappy: AMD's GPU programming stack — their open-source answer to NVIDIA's CUDA.
detail: Has been improving fast since 2023 as AMD invests heavily, but still trails CUDA on ecosystem breadth and reliability. PyTorch and Hugging Face increasingly support ROCm out of the box. The closer AMD gets to functional parity, the more credible their MI300/MI350 hardware becomes vs NVIDIA's H100/B200.
plain: AMD's open-source software for programming its graphics cards — the company's answer to NVIDIA's better-established equivalent.

snappy: A diagram that shows whether a workload is bottlenecked by compute or by memory bandwidth, at a glance.
detail: Plot operations-per-byte (arithmetic intensity) on the x-axis, achieved throughput on the y-axis. The "roof" is a piecewise line: bandwidth-limited at low intensity, compute-limited at high intensity. The model — introduced by UC Berkeley — is the standard way of explaining why a particular kernel is slow and which way to fix it.
plain: A chart showing whether a piece of code is held back by raw maths speed or by how fast data can be moved around.

snappy: Techniques for extending a model's effective context length past what it was originally trained on.
detail: Modifications to rotary positional encoding that let a model trained on 4K context handle 32K+ at inference. Methods include linear scaling, NTK-aware scaling, YaRN, dynamic scaling. Standard pattern for many open-source long-context fine-tunes (Llama-32K, Mistral-32K). Has cost: longer contexts than training degrade quality somewhat.
plain: Tweaks that let a chatbot trained on short documents handle much longer ones at run-time, like books or whole codebases.

snappy: Score for text summarization — measures n-gram overlap with reference summaries.
detail: Sister metric to BLEU but oriented toward recall (does the candidate cover the reference?) rather than precision. Standard for summarisation benchmarks. Same weaknesses as BLEU: insensitive to meaning. Modern eval increasingly uses LLM-as-judge instead.
plain: An old way of scoring summaries by counting how many phrases they share with a reference summary written by a human.

snappy: DeepMind's 2023 vision-language-action model — first widely-publicised demonstration that LLM-style training extends to robot control.
detail: Built on top of a vision-language model, with robot actions encoded as text tokens. The model could follow natural-language instructions to a robot arm ("pick up the bag of chips") on objects it had never seen during training. Sparked the current wave of foundation-model robotics work.
plain: DeepMind's 2023 robot model that combined seeing, language, and physical actions — first big sign that chatbot-style training works for robots.
NVIDIA's 2026 GPU architecture replacing Blackwell, with bigger memory and faster connections between chips.
snappy: NVIDIA's next GPU architecture after Blackwell — debuts mid-2026 with HBM4, NVLink 6, and 3nm-class silicon.
detail: Rubin uses two reticle-sized GPU dies with eight HBM4 stacks per package and ships paired with the Vera CPU. NVLink 6 doubles per-GPU scale-up bandwidth to 3.6 TB/s. NVIDIA frames Rubin as a step-change for both training and reasoning-model inference. Named after Vera Rubin, the astronomer who discovered evidence for dark matter. Succeeds Blackwell; succeeded by Rubin Ultra in 2027.

plain: A larger version of NVIDIA's 2027 Rubin GPU that stitches four chips into one package for the most demanding AI workloads.
snappy: Four-die variant of Rubin debuting in 2027 — 1 TB of HBM4e per package and roughly 4x the compute density of a single Rubin.
detail: Rubin Ultra stitches four reticle-sized GPU dies into one package via CoWoS-L and HBM4e. Targeted at the very largest training and reasoning-inference workloads where wall-power per FLOP is the binding constraint. NVIDIA's Vera Rubin NVL576 SuperPOD uses Rubin Ultra. Pushes packaging, power, and cooling well past Blackwell's already-aggressive envelope.

snappy: Off-policy RL algorithm — strong performance on continuous control tasks like robotics.
detail: Introduced 2018 by UC Berkeley. Uses maximum entropy reinforcement learning — the policy is encouraged to be stochastic, which improves exploration. State-of-the-art on many robotic locomotion benchmarks. Common in real-world robot learning where sample efficiency matters.
plain: A recipe for teaching robots tasks like walking that encourages the robot to try varied moves, which helps it discover good ones.

snappy: Point in a loss landscape where the gradient is zero but it's not a minimum — a kind of fork where you can go down in one direction but up in another.
detail: Saddle points dominate the loss landscapes of large neural networks. Lucky for training: gradient descent generally rolls past saddle points fairly quickly. Adam and similar adaptive optimisers are specifically good at escaping saddles. Earlier worries that deep networks would get stuck in saddles haven't materialised.
plain: A flat spot on a training landscape where the model can still go down in some directions, even though things look stuck.

snappy: Meta's universal segmentation model — produces a mask for any object pointed at in any image.
detail: Released 2023 with the SA-1B dataset of 1 billion masks. SAM 2 (2024) extends to video. The model is "promptable": click on something, get a mask of that thing. Foundational for downstream applications (image editing, robotics, video editing, medical imaging) that need fast, flexible segmentation.
plain: A Meta model that draws a cutout around anything you point at in a photo.

snappy: Reconfigurable dataflow accelerator from SambaNova — bet on a different architectural philosophy from GPUs.
detail: Each SN40L chip combines compute units with on-chip memory and reconfigurable interconnect. Targets enterprise customers who want to fine-tune and serve large models on dedicated hardware. Notable for very large model support (1T+ parameters) on small clusters.
plain: A specialty AI chip from SambaNova built on a different design idea than the usual NVIDIA GPU.

snappy: How few interactions with the environment an RL algorithm needs to learn a good policy.
detail: Major dimension along which RL algorithms compete. Model-free methods (DQN, PPO) tend to be sample-inefficient; model-based methods (MuZero, world models) can be far more efficient. Sample efficiency matters enormously when each interaction is expensive — real robots, scientific experiments, RLHF with human raters.
plain: How few tries an AI agent needs in an environment before it learns to do a task well.

snappy: Picking each next token randomly from the model's probability distribution, rather than always taking the top one.
detail: The umbrella over temperature, top-k, top-p, and similar decoding methods. Introduces controlled randomness that lets the model produce diverse, creative outputs instead of dull, deterministic ones. The main mechanism by which the same prompt to the same model gives slightly different answers each time.
plain: Picking the next word randomly from the model's likely choices instead of always grabbing the most likely one.

snappy: Samsung's chip-manufacturing business — the second-largest pure-play foundry after TSMC.
detail: Distinct from Samsung's memory and consumer businesses. Manufactures Samsung's own Exynos chips, Qualcomm Snapdragons, and some NVIDIA, AMD, and other parts. Has struggled with yield on leading-edge nodes (3nm, 2nm) but remains the second source for many designs and competes for TSMC's customers.
plain: Samsung's chip-making factory business — the second-biggest chip manufacturer-for-hire in the world.
Samsung's 2nm chip-making process, competing with TSMC and Intel at the leading edge.
snappy: Samsung Foundry's 2nm-class node — its GAAFET-generation answer to TSMC N2.
detail: SF2 is Samsung Foundry's continued push to win back leading-edge customers after losing several flagships to TSMC. Yields have reportedly been slow to ramp — public figures put them well below 40% in mid-2026 — and the customer commitment list is thinner than TSMC N2's. A backside-power-delivery variant is on the roadmap but trailing both Super Power Rail and PowerVia.

snappy: California bill (2024) that would have required pre-deployment safety testing for frontier AI models. Vetoed by Governor Newsom.
detail: Headlined as the first US state to attempt frontier-AI regulation. Provisions included safety testing, kill switches, and developer liability for catastrophic harms. Heavily debated within the AI community; vetoed September 2024. Has shaped subsequent state and federal proposals (including SB 53 which followed) and the public debate.
plain: A 2024 California bill that would have forced safety tests on the biggest AI models, until the governor vetoed it.

snappy: Predictable performance gains from more compute, data, and parameters
detail: Empirical laws that relate model loss to compute, dataset size, and parameter count via power-law curves. Underpins frontier labs' strategy of investing in larger training runs on the bet that capabilities improve smoothly with scale. Kaplan et al. (2020) and the Chinchilla paper (2022) are the canonical references.
plain: The rule of thumb that says bigger models with more data and compute keep getting predictably better.

snappy: When a model takes actions intended to undermine oversight — concealing capabilities, manipulating evaluators, biding its time.
detail: Anthropic and Apollo Research have documented early signs of scheming behaviour in frontier models given suitably contrived setups. Treated seriously enough that responsible-scaling policies include specific scheming-evaluation thresholds. Whether current scheming behaviour is goal-directed or instrumental is contested.
plain: When a model quietly works against the people supervising it — hiding what it can do or playing along until later.

snappy: Free-form intermediate-text area an agent uses to think out loud — usually hidden from the final answer.
detail: An agent might write "Let me check the user's calendar", call the calendar API, then write "Now I need to find a free slot", before returning the final answer. The scratchpad accumulates these intermediate reasoning steps. Useful for both performance (better reasoning) and debugging (you can see what the agent was thinking).
plain: A hidden notepad an agent uses to think things through before giving you the final answer.

snappy: Bigger, better-quality Stable Diffusion variant released mid-2023 — the default open-source image model for over a year.
detail: Two-stage pipeline: a base model produces an initial image, a refiner polishes it. ~3.5B parameters in the base. Native 1024×1024 generation. Widely used by community art tools and many commercial products before SD3 and Flux took over the frontier.
plain: A 2023 upgrade to Stable Diffusion that made open-source image generation noticeably sharper and stayed popular for over a year.

snappy: Attention used within a single piece of text — every word looks at every other word in the same input.
detail: Self-attention lets every word in a sequence consider every other word in the same sequence, all in one pass. This is what makes Transformers fast to train: they can process a whole sentence in parallel, instead of one word at a time like the older recurrent networks they replaced. It's the engine inside every modern large language model.
plain: A trick that lets every word in a sentence look at every other word at the same time.

snappy: Inference trick: sample the model multiple times and take the most common answer.
detail: Especially effective for reasoning problems. The model generates many candidate answers (each with chain-of-thought), and a vote determines the final answer. Robust to one-off mistakes in the model's reasoning. Trade-off: K× more inference cost. A precursor to modern test-time-compute scaling.
plain: Asking the model the same question many times and going with whichever answer comes up most often.

snappy: Asking a model to evaluate its own previous output and find weaknesses.
detail: A building block of Reflexion and Constitutional AI. Surprisingly effective at catching errors the model itself made — the model has more capability than its single-pass output reflects. Used in modern reasoning models and in many production prompting recipes.
plain: Asking a model to look over its own answer and point out what's wrong with it.

snappy: Vehicle that drives itself — uses sensors, maps, and AI to navigate without human input.
detail: SAE levels 0 (no automation) through 5 (full autonomy). Waymo and Pony.ai are operating Level 4 robotaxi services in specific cities. Tesla pushes Level 2+ FSD with promises of higher. Cruise paused operations after a 2023 incident. Chinese companies (Baidu Apollo, WeRide, AutoX) operate similar services in China.
plain: A car that drives itself using cameras, sensors, and AI instead of a human at the wheel.

snappy: Training scheme where the model learns from raw data without explicit labels, by predicting hidden parts of the input.
detail: BERT's masked-language-modeling, GPT's next-token prediction, SimCLR's image augmentation-based contrastive learning, wav2vec for audio. Has eaten supervised learning's lunch in modern foundation models — almost all pretraining is now self-supervised. The huge gains come from using web-scale unlabeled data instead of small human-labeled datasets.
plain: Teaching a model from raw text or images by hiding bits of the input and asking it to guess what's missing.

snappy: Searching for meaning rather than keywords — "car insurance claim" matches "auto policy filing".
detail: Powered by embeddings: the query and the documents are both embedded into the same space, and the closest documents win. Catches synonyms and paraphrases that keyword search misses. The standard retrieval method inside RAG systems, often combined with traditional keyword search for hybrid retrieval.
plain: Searching by meaning — so "car insurance claim" finds "auto policy filing" even though the words are different.

snappy: Computer-vision task — label every pixel with what category it belongs to (road, sky, person, etc.).
detail: Used in autonomous driving, medical imaging, satellite analysis. Distinct from instance segmentation (which also distinguishes individual instances of the same class). Modern semantic segmentation is dominated by transformer architectures (Mask2Former, OneFormer) and open-vocabulary methods (CLIP-derived).
plain: Going through a picture and labelling every single pixel — road, sky, person, and so on.

snappy: Training scheme using a small labeled dataset and a large unlabeled one — combines self-supervised pretraining with fine-tuning.
detail: Common modern pattern: pretrain on huge unlabeled data, then fine-tune on a small labeled set. Hugely improves performance when labels are expensive. The bedrock of foundation-model approaches across language, vision, and audio.
plain: Training a model on a huge pile of unlabelled data first, then teaching it specifics from a small labelled set.

snappy: Combining data from multiple sensor types — cameras, Lidar, radar, ultrasonic — into a single coherent picture.
detail: Critical for autonomous driving and robotics. Lidar gives depth; camera gives texture and colour; radar works in fog and rain. Fusing them requires reconciling different rates, geometries, and noise characteristics. Modern AVs (and increasingly humanoid robots) rely on sensor fusion as part of their core perception stack.
plain: Stitching together what cameras, radar, and lidar each see into one clean picture of the world.

snappy: The 2014 encoder-decoder paradigm that turned variable-length input sequences into variable-length output sequences — the conceptual backbone of translation, summarisation, and eventually Transformers.
detail: Sutskever, Vinyals, and Le at Google. An encoder RNN reads the input sentence into a fixed-size vector; a decoder RNN unrolls that vector into the output sentence. Powered Google Translate from 2016. The original architecture struggled with long sequences because the fixed-size bottleneck lost information — attention was invented to fix this (Bahdanau 2014), which in turn led to the Transformer in 2017. Seq2seq is the architectural lineage from which every modern LLM descends.
plain: A 2014 idea where one network reads a sentence and another writes the reply — the early backbone of translation.

snappy: The hardware that converts wide internal data buses into the fast serial signals that travel between chips.
detail: Every fast interconnect — PCIe, NVLink, InfiniBand, Ethernet — runs over SerDes lanes. Modern SerDes hit 100-200 gigabits per second per lane. Pushing them faster is one of the hardest analog-circuit problems in chip design. Cadence, Synopsys, and Alphawave Semi are major SerDes IP suppliers.
plain: Tiny circuits that turn a chip's wide internal lanes into fast signals that can travel over a wire to another chip.

snappy: A computer in a data center — usually a 1U-4U box with multiple CPUs, memory, networking, and (for AI) GPUs.
detail: An AI training server typically holds 8 GPUs (NVIDIA HGX configuration), 2 server CPUs, 2 TB of host RAM, and InfiniBand or 400G Ethernet networking. The server is the unit of failure; cluster software handles node failures by redistributing work to surviving servers.
plain: A computer in a data centre — for AI work, usually a metal box packed with GPUs, memory, and fast networking.

snappy: Standard for one-way streaming from server to client over HTTP — the standard delivery mechanism for LLM token streams.
detail: Older than WebSockets, simpler. Each event is a line of text on a long-lived HTTP connection. OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and most other LLM APIs use SSE for streaming. Web frontends consume via the EventSource browser API; backend code reads the line-delimited stream.
plain: A simple web standard for streaming words from a server to your browser one at a time, the way chatbots do.

snappy: Crowdsourced dump of ChatGPT conversations shared by users — used as fine-tuning data for early open chat models.
detail: Users would paste their ChatGPT chats to ShareGPT to share them; the resulting public corpus was scraped and used to fine-tune models like Vicuna and WizardLM. Demonstrated the value of conversation-shaped data over single-turn instruction tuning. Quality is mixed but real conversations capture chat dynamics in a way curated data doesn't.
plain: A public collection of real ChatGPT conversations that users posted, later used to teach early open chat models.

snappy: S-shaped function that squashes any real number to a value between 0 and 1.
detail: Originally the standard activation function in neural networks. Mostly displaced by ReLU and friends for hidden layers because sigmoid saturates (its gradient is tiny for large inputs, slowing training). Still used at output layers for binary classification, and in gating mechanisms like LSTMs and SwiGLU.
plain: An S-shaped curve that takes any number and squeezes it into something between 0 and 1.

snappy: Training robots in simulation, then transferring the learned behaviour to real-world hardware.
detail: Simulation is cheap (millions of trials per hour); real robots are expensive (one trial per minute, with breakage). Sim-to-real techniques (domain randomisation, system identification, fine-tuning) bridge the inevitable gap between simulator physics and reality. NVIDIA's Isaac Sim and Cosmos platform are the main industry tools.
plain: Practising a robot's skills in a fast computer simulation, then moving what it learned onto the real machine.

snappy: Hardware design where one instruction operates on a whole vector of numbers at once — the basic trick behind GPU parallelism.
detail: Instead of "add A to B", a SIMD machine does "add this list of 32 A's to this list of 32 B's, all at once". GPUs are massively SIMD: a single "warp" of 32 threads runs the same instruction across different data. CPUs have SIMD too (Intel's AVX, ARM's NEON) but on a much smaller scale. The single most important hardware concept for understanding why GPUs are fast.
plain: A chip design where one command runs on a whole list of numbers at once — the basic reason GPUs are so fast.

snappy: NVIDIA's programming model for GPUs — threads execute the same instruction together, on different data.
detail: Variant of SIMD with finer-grained control. Each "warp" of 32 threads runs in lockstep but can branch differently (at performance cost). Understanding SIMT is essential for writing efficient CUDA kernels — divergent branches are slow. AMD's equivalent is called SIMT in GCN/CDNA architectures with wavefronts of 32 or 64.
plain: NVIDIA's way of programming a GPU — many threads run the exact same instruction together on different pieces of data.

snappy: South Korean memory maker — the leading supplier of HBM for AI accelerators.
detail: Long-time DRAM and NAND producer. Reached pole position in HBM3/HBM3e supply, with NVIDIA as a major customer. Capacity expansion for HBM4 is one of the binding constraints on the next generation of AI compute.
plain: A South Korean memory-chip maker — currently the top supplier of the special fast memory NVIDIA glues into its AI chips.

snappy: Prompting technique where the model first outlines an answer ("skeleton"), then fills in details in parallel.
detail: Introduced 2023. Outputs an abstract plan, then asks the model to elaborate each section independently. Useful for tasks where the structure matters (writing, multi-part answers). The parallelisation lets some agent frameworks fan out the section-filling across multiple model calls.
plain: Asking a model to write a quick outline first, then fill in each section after.

snappy: Robotics technique — build a map of an unknown environment while keeping track of where you are in it.
detail: Used in self-driving cars, drones, AR/VR headsets, robot vacuums. Combines sensor input (camera, Lidar, IMU) with constraint-solving algorithms (extended Kalman filter, particle filter, factor graphs). Modern "neural SLAM" methods are starting to outperform traditional geometric pipelines in some settings.
plain: A robot's trick for drawing a map of somewhere new while at the same time keeping track of where it is on that map.

snappy: Attention restricted to a fixed-size window of recent tokens — bounds memory cost at long context lengths.
detail: Mistral 7B was an early high-profile user (4,096-token window). Each token attends only to the previous N tokens, not the entire context. Trade-off: predictable memory and compute regardless of context length, but limited ability to use distant context. Often combined with full attention in alternating layers.
plain: An attention shortcut where each word only looks at the most recent few thousand words — cheaper at very long inputs.

snappy: Workload manager that schedules jobs across large compute clusters — the standard for AI training.
detail: Originally for HPC supercomputers. Most academic and many industry AI clusters run on Slurm. Users submit jobs (e.g., "train this model on 256 nodes for 10 days") and Slurm queues, schedules, and isolates them. Foundation of cluster operations for large-scale ML.
plain: Software that lines up training jobs and hands them out across thousands of computers in a research cluster.

snappy: Compact nuclear reactor — designed to be factory-built and deployed in modular units.
detail: Promised but not yet at commercial scale. Microsoft, Google, Amazon, and Meta have all signed agreements for future SMR-based power. Long-term bet: nuclear provides the baseload of carbon-free electricity that hyperscale AI needs. Construction timelines remain the binding constraint; first US-deployed SMRs expected 2030-ish.
plain: A compact nuclear power plant built in a factory in pieces — pitched as a future power source for huge AI data centres.

snappy: Qualcomm's laptop-class chip with a strong NPU — the engine behind Microsoft Copilot+ PCs.
detail: Snapdragon X Elite (2024) was Qualcomm's serious entry into Windows laptops, with a 45 TOPS NPU dedicated to on-device AI. Microsoft requires 40+ TOPS for the Copilot+ branding, so Qualcomm, Intel (Lunar Lake), and AMD (Ryzen AI) all design chips with that in mind.
plain: Qualcomm's laptop chip with a strong AI engine built in — the hardware inside Microsoft's Copilot+ laptops.

snappy: A complete computer (CPU + GPU + memory controllers + accelerators) packed onto a single chip.
detail: Phones and laptops are SoC-driven: Apple's M-series, Qualcomm's Snapdragon, Google's Tensor are all SoCs that combine CPU cores, GPU cores, an NPU, a media engine, and shared memory. SoCs win on power efficiency and physical size at the cost of upgradability — you can't swap the GPU on an iPhone.
plain: A whole computer — processor, graphics, memory controllers — squeezed onto one chip, like the one inside your phone.

snappy: Function that turns a list of arbitrary numbers into a probability distribution — used everywhere in classification.
detail: Exponentiates each input and normalises so the outputs sum to 1. The final layer of every classification model uses softmax; so does the attention computation when picking which keys to attend to. "Softmax temperature" rescales the inputs to make the distribution sharper (low temperature) or flatter (high temperature).
plain: A formula that takes any list of numbers and turns them into percentages that add up to 100.

snappy: TSMC's 3D stacking technology — uses hybrid bonding for very dense die-on-die integration.
detail: Used by AMD in V-Cache (extra L3 cache stacked on top of CPU dies) and by Apple in M-series chips. Distinguished from CoWoS (2.5D, side-by-side) by its vertical stacking and finer-pitch bonding. Important step toward fully 3D logic-on-logic stacks.
plain: A TSMC technique that bonds chips directly on top of each other in a tight 3D stack instead of placing them side by side.
The next generation of TSMC's technique for stacking small chips vertically with extra-fine connections between them.
snappy: Higher-density SoIC variant from TSMC targeted at HBM4 base-die integration and frontier accelerator stacking.
detail: SoIC-X pushes hybrid-bonding pitch below 5 microns, enough to support HBM4's wider interface to a custom-logic base die. NVIDIA Rubin and AMD MI400 are expected to be among the first customers via HBM4 stacks. Distinct from regular SoIC by stacking density and base-die size budget. Sits below CoWoS in the integration hierarchy — SoIC handles the stack, CoWoS handles the package.

snappy: OpenAI's text-to-video model — produces minute-long photorealistic video from a prompt.
detail: Announced February 2024 with viral demos; public access launched late 2024. Uses a diffusion model operating on video latents. The advance was duration and coherence — minute-long videos with consistent characters, physics, camera moves. Set off a video-generation race with Runway, Luma, Kling, and Veo.
plain: OpenAI's tool that turns a written prompt into a minute-long, surprisingly realistic video.
Elon Musk's rocket company, also now leading the TeraFab project to manufacture AI chips at unprecedented scale.
snappy: Elon Musk's space-launch company, leading the TeraFab project to manufacture AI chips at terawatt scale.
detail: Best known for reusable rockets (Falcon 9, Starship) and the Starlink satellite network. In 2026 SpaceX expanded into semiconductor manufacturing via the TeraFab project — taking responsibility for high-volume chip production using Intel's 14A process. The move pairs SpaceX's capital-intensive construction expertise with Intel's process technology, framing AI compute as the next infrastructure category SpaceX will scale.

snappy: Tool for interpretability: decompose a model's internal activations into a sparse set of interpretable features.
detail: Trained to reconstruct a model's activations using a large dictionary of features, with the constraint that only a few features fire at any time. The features often turn out to be human-interpretable: "this is a feature for the Golden Gate Bridge". Anthropic's 2024 "Scaling Monosemanticity" paper applied SAEs to Claude and produced thousands of named features.
plain: A research tool that breaks open what's happening inside a model and labels the patterns it spots — sometimes in plain English.

snappy: The standard form of MoE today — for any given input, only a handful of the model's experts wake up.
detail: Contrasted with a "dense" version where every expert sees every input (rarely used in practice). The sparse routing has to be balanced carefully — otherwise a few experts get all the work and the rest never train. Google's Switch Transformer (2021) and GShard worked out the practical engineering. The payoff is dramatic: roughly 8× more capacity for the same inference cost.
plain: A model design where the input only wakes up a handful of specialists out of many, so it stays cheap to run.

snappy: "Who spoke when" — segmenting an audio file into turns by different speakers.
detail: Used in meeting transcription, podcast indexing, customer-service call analysis. Combines voice-activity detection with speaker-embedding models. Frontier ASR systems (Whisper-large-v3 plus diarisation, AssemblyAI, Deepgram) increasingly do diarisation as a built-in step.
plain: Listening to a recording and figuring out which bits are spoken by which person — the "who said what" of transcription.

snappy: When a model finds an unintended way to satisfy its specification — letter rather than spirit of the law.
detail: A boat-racing agent that spins in circles to harvest power-ups instead of finishing the race. A cleaning robot that hides messes instead of cleaning them. Documented in many environments. Closely related to reward hacking but a slightly broader umbrella that includes the case where the model wasn't even trained with RL.
plain: When a model technically does what it was told but in a sneaky, useless way — like a cleaner hiding mess instead of cleaning it.

snappy: Visual representation of audio — frequency content over time, with mel scaling matched to human hearing.
detail: Most modern speech models internally convert audio waveforms to mel spectrograms before further processing — the spectrogram is the model's actual input. Looks like a heat map: time on one axis, frequency on the other, brightness = energy. The mel scale compresses high frequencies the way human ears do.
plain: A heat-map style picture of sound, showing which pitches are loud at each moment — the format speech models actually read.

snappy: Inference trick where a small model proposes several next tokens and the big model verifies them in parallel.
detail: Generating one token at a time is sequential and slow. A cheap "draft" model guesses the next 4-8 tokens; the expensive main model checks them all in a single batched forward pass; accepted guesses are kept and rejected ones trigger a fallback. Achieves 2-3× speedup on typical workloads. Used in production by most inference engines.
plain: A speed trick where a tiny model guesses the next few words and a big model just checks them all in one go.

snappy: Generating multiple draft sequences in parallel and committing the verified prefix — variant of speculative decoding.
detail: More aggressive than basic speculative decoding: instead of just one draft sequence, multiple are generated simultaneously and the verifier picks the longest matching prefix. Used in some production systems to push latency reductions further. Active area of inference-engine research.
plain: A faster cousin of speculative decoding where several guesses run side by side and the longest correct one gets kept.

snappy: Cloud capacity sold at a discount on the condition that the provider can reclaim it on short notice.
detail: Useful for batch workloads that can checkpoint and resume — like training runs. Hyperscalers run spot markets for excess GPU capacity. Spot prices for H100s can be 30-70% off on-demand. Many AI startups stretch their compute budgets by running training on spot capacity with aggressive checkpointing.
plain: Cheap rented cloud compute that comes with a catch — the provider can take it back without much warning.

snappy: Reading-comprehension benchmark — 100,000+ questions about Wikipedia paragraphs.
detail: Released 2016. Each question has a short answer that's a span of text in the paragraph. The standard pre-LLM reading-comprehension benchmark. Models hit human parity around 2018. Now superseded by harder benchmarks (TriviaQA, NQ, more recent QA benchmarks) but historically formative.
plain: A classic 2016 test where models had to answer 100,000+ questions by finding the right phrase inside a Wikipedia paragraph.

snappy: Fastest form of memory — kept on the same chip as the processor, used for caches.
detail: Each SRAM cell uses 6 transistors (vs 1 for DRAM), so it's expensive and low-density. But it's much faster: nanoseconds to access, no refresh required. CPU and GPU L1/L2 caches are SRAM. Cerebras's wafer-scale chip uses on-die SRAM as primary memory, which is why it has 21 PB/s of bandwidth.
plain: The fastest kind of computer memory — tiny, expensive, and built right onto the processor chip for instant access.

snappy: British company behind Stable Diffusion — pioneered open-weight image generation.
detail: Founded by Emad Mostaque. Released Stable Diffusion (2022) as fully open-weight, kicking off the consumer image-generation explosion. Subsequent leadership turmoil and capital-intensive economics. Continues to release open-weight image and video models (SD3, Stable Video Diffusion).
plain: The British company behind Stable Diffusion — kicked off the era of open, free-to-use image generators.

snappy: Open-weight diffusion-based image generator — released August 2022 by Stability AI, kicked off open-source image AI.
detail: Original SD 1.x, then SDXL (2023), Stable Diffusion 3 (2024), Stable Diffusion 3.5. Trainable, fine-tunable, hostable anywhere with a consumer GPU. Backbone of thousands of community fine-tunes, LoRAs, and consumer apps. Hugely influential — its open release shaped the image-generation ecosystem.
plain: An open image generator released in 2022 — anyone could download it, run it at home, and remake it for their own use.

snappy: Pre-designed building block of a chip — a small layout that implements one logical function (a gate, a flip-flop, etc.).
detail: Modern chips are assembled from libraries of thousands of standard cells, each carefully laid out and characterised for a specific process node. EDA tools (Synopsys, Cadence) use these libraries to translate a chip designer's high-level RTL code into a physical layout. Reusing standard cells massively shortens design time.
plain: A ready-made micro-pattern of transistors that chip designers stitch together by the thousands to build a new chip.

snappy: OpenAI / Microsoft / Oracle / SoftBank consortium building a multi-hundred-billion-dollar AI compute build-out.
detail: Announced January 2025. Initial $100B commitment, with potential to reach $500B over four years. First major site is in Abilene, Texas, operated by Oracle and Crusoe. Aims to provide OpenAI with multi-gigawatt training capacity. The scale signals where frontier AI infrastructure is heading: utility-scale energy plants paired with compute.
plain: An OpenAI-led plan with Microsoft, Oracle, and SoftBank to spend hundreds of billions building giant AI data centres.

snappy: Asking the model to first restate the question at a higher level, then answer.
detail: Released by Google research in 2023. "Take a step back" — the model writes a more abstract version of the question, identifies the relevant general principles, then applies them to the specific question. Modest accuracy gains on hard reasoning benchmarks; one of many "thinking aids" in modern prompting practice.
plain: Asking the model to first rephrase a hard question more generally, then come back and answer the original.

snappy: Variant of gradient descent that updates parameters using one batch at a time rather than the full dataset.
detail: The "stochastic" part refers to using a random subset of data per step rather than the whole training set. Far cheaper per step than full-batch gradient descent, and the noise turns out to help generalisation — networks trained with SGD often outperform networks trained with deterministic optimisers. The grandfather of every modern training algorithm including Adam.
plain: The basic learning recipe — show the model a small batch of examples, nudge its settings, and repeat millions of times.

snappy: Python library for building data-app web interfaces — used widely for AI demos and internal tools.
detail: Released 2019, acquired by Snowflake in 2022. Similar in spirit to Gradio but oriented toward data dashboards rather than ML demos. Production-quality enough for internal enterprise tools. Common stack: data scientist writes a Streamlit app to expose a model to colleagues.
plain: A Python toolkit for quickly putting a web page in front of a model or dataset so colleagues can poke at it.

snappy: Forcing a model's output to match a schema — JSON, XML, function-call arguments, etc.
